messages.subject: g++ version; un-/re-installing R packages
messages.body_plain:
Question 1
----------
Does anyone know how to control the version of
g++ used by R?  The default version shipped with the
Mac isn't up to our template defaults yet, but it's
easy to install a new compiler that is.  I'd like to
tell R to use that one.

Otherwise, I think we're going to have to bite the
bullet and duplicate every function in our probability
lib to deal with defaults (this is, by the way, what
Boost does -- the core problem is that without the c++0x
extensions, you can't have a template parameter default
for a function.

Question 2
----------
How do I work with R when developing packages so
that I can uninstall and reinstall a package without
quitting R?

I managed to get Rcpp modules linking to the Stan
code, but I can't figure out how to get R to forget
about the last version and load the new one.

I can create my Rcpp module-based package using their
template as follows

   SHELL
   $ R CMD build mypkg
   $ R CMD check mypkg
   $ R CMD install mypkg

   R
   > require("mypkg")
   > foo(2,3)

That all works fine, with foo(2,3) being
defined in my package.  But then I change some code
and rebuild and reinstall the package

   SHELL
   $ R CMD remove mypkg
   $ R CMD build mypkg
   $ R CMD check mypkg
   $ R CMD install mypkg

And then I go into R and do this:

   R
   > detach("package:mypkg")
   > require("mypkg")

and I get the old version.  If I then quit out of R
and start again, I get the new one without going back
to the shell, etc.

There's so much noise on the R lists about installing
packages that I can't find a single useful bit of advice.

- Bob

If you just need to test modified R code, you can usually just paste it into the R session. But if you modify source code, it is easiest to quit R, reinstall the package, and restart R.

messages.body_plain:
I'm beginning to think an R2WinBUGS-like completely
external approach will not only be easiest, but also
most robust to the vagaries of R's package manager's
approach to building and loading/unloading.

I'm also worried about g++ version, etc., because of
the compilation problems we've had on Windows overall
and our reliance on C++11 features which aren't supported
by the standard g++ on the Mac OSX as used by the most
recent R.  Not to mention older versions of R.

That'd involve the following steps from R's perspective:

   a.  write data and inits to file from R:
       : R dump:
   b.  compile Stan model to C++
       : R system: run Stan compiler (now demo/gm)
   c.  compile C++ to an executable
       : R system: run C++ compiler
   d.  run compiled model with data/inits and write
       output into a file
       : R system: run compiled executable
   e.  read the data from the file back into R
       : R read.csv

It's super crude, but it gets us outside of having to
depend on R's build and load/unload package management
mechanisms.

Now here's some more on some back and forth Ben and I
have been having about load/unload causing a segfault
(dozens if not hundreds of message boards reports of
such, no answers I could find).

On 3/2/12 10:36 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 > I am guessing
 >
 > dyn.load()
 > dyn.unload()
 >
 > are going to be needed.

I'm really unsure about how to go about this.
The problem is that we want to be able to unload
and the reload the same thing.

I've tried reading through the R Extensions Manual several
times, but I still can't quite put all the pieces together.
Section 5.3 suggests putting useDynLib() in NAMESPACE,
but Rcpp's already done that for us in its skeleton.
Do I then need to use library.dynam() to load?  If so,
how do I figure out what "libname" to use?
It says it's the name of the dll, but I don't see where
I can control making a dynamic lib.  The doc
points to SHLIB.  But then the doc there says it's already
being called by INSTALL.  So I don't see what we're missing.

 > It still isn't completely clear to me how we are
 > going to get the model to the model. I guess one approach would be to
 > define the module in rstan/src/module.hpp and then use inline with
 > includes = "rstan/src/module.hpp".

If we call inline, what does it do to load/unload
the C++ code?  We're imagining people redefining and
recompiling their models.  I was thinking we'd be able to
put the compiled C++ code into something that looked like
an R package through Rcpp and then dynamically reload
it when the user changes the model.  I could just keep
generating new names, but it doesn't look like R's freeing
resources (or maybe it's just the pointers to the
resources that linger to cause the segfaults?).

I haven't looked into R's threading or multiple process
control, but we'd like to run four parallel chains in
most cases.

- Bob

I'm doing wrong:

messages.subject: biting bullet on C++11
messages.body_plain:
I'm going in and removing all of our
reliance on C++11 features.  As far as
I know, that's only using default template
parameters for functions.  At least I'm going
to start there.

Most (all?) of the work's in the densities,
which currently look like:

   template <bool propto = false,
             typename T1, ..., typename TN,
             class Policy=default::type>
   return_type<T1,...,TN>::type
   foo_log(T1 x1, ..., TN xn, Policy& = Policy()) {
       ...
   }

The tricky bit here is the &= Policy() bit coupled
with the template default Policy=default::type.

First, there's no argument name for the last argument.
But there is a default value, Policy(). This
sleight-of-hand ensures that we never need to do
any work passing policy arguments to foo() at runtime.
At compile time, we only need the type of the argument in
order to infer the parameter type.  If we ever need
a policy, we just pass Policy(), most likely to another
function that only cares about the type.  The cool
part is no work at runtime at all.

All very clever, but too much for pre C++-11 compilers,
like the defaults for R on the Mac (Mac OS X is way behind
the rest of the world in default compiler g++/clang++
versions; and Apple very annoyingly want you to upgrade Mac
OS version to get the latest tools).

What I'll need to do is replace the above with one full function:

   template <bool propto,
             typename T1, ..., typename TN,
             class Policy>
   return_type<T1,...,TN>::type
   foo_log(T1 x1, ..., TN xn, Policy& /* */) {
       ...
   }

and one inlinable function which instantiates the
default policy and calls the above:

   template <bool propto,
             typename T1, ..., typename TN>
   inline
   return_type<T1,...,TN>::type
   foo_log(T1 x1, ..., TN xn) {
      return foo<propto>(x1,...,xn,default_policy::type());
   }

The downside is that the propto value will need to be
instantiated explicitly.  So anywhere we used to write

   foo_log(x,y,z);

we'll now have to write:

   foo_log<false>(x,y,z);

to let the compiler know that we don't intend prop-to calcs, but
full probability calcs.  Where we used to write foo_log<true>(...)
can stay the same.  I sort of like that this makes the proptos
explicit.  I can add constants, so that we would write

    foo_log<propto>(x,y,z) =def=  foo_log<true>(x,y,z);

    foo_log<full>(x,y,z);  =def=  foo_log<false>(x,y,z);

We could go back to our existing default behavior
by adding two more inlines (which still call the
one-true implementation):

   template <typename T1, ..., typename TN>
   inline
   return_type<T1,...,TN>::type
   foo_log(T1 x1, ..., TN xn) {
      return foo_log<false>(x1,...,xn,default_policy::type());
       ...
   }

and

   template <typename T1, ..., typename TN,
             class Policy>
   inline
   return_type<T1,...,TN>::type
   foo_log(T1 x1, ..., TN xn, Policy& /* */) {
     return foo_log<false>(x1,...,xN,Policy());
   }

- Bob

  duplicate functions to remove Policy default,
     a la Boost.

One complication is that all of our densities
will have to be called with an explicit first
template parameter

So I've pulled stan from git and have been playing around with specifying a time series model.  I've run into an issue and I'm not sure if it's a bug or if I'm just doing something silly.

It's a simple AR model and the specification has the line:

lambda[t] ~ multi_normal( diag_matrix(1-phi)*mu + diag_matrix(phi)*lambda[t-1], U );

where lambda, phi and mu are vectors and U is a cov_matrix.

The parser chokes with:

    lambda[t] ~ multi_normal( diag_matrix(1-phi)*mu + diag_matrix(phi)*lambda[t-1], U );
                                                               ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

expression is ill formed
Parser expecting: <eps>

Any suggestions?  I've tried a number of different variations on the expression, including defining transformed variables to represent the mean to no avail.

Also, on a related note, has anyone created a time-series demo for stan?  If not I'd be more than happy to contribute this one once I get it running.

Cheers,
Marcus

OK. We are getting closer (at least on my Linux laptop).

Do this in bash:

export STAN_HOME=/opt/stan; # or wherever stan lives
cd $STAN_HOME/src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker/
cat blocker.stan | $STAN_HOME/demo/gm > blocker.cpp
export PKG_CXXFLAGS="-I/opt/stan/src -I/opt/stan/lib -std=c++0x"

Now do this in R from the blocker/ directory:

is.loaded("main") # FALSE
dyn.load("blocker.so")
is.loaded("main") # TRUE
dyn.unload("blocker.so")
is.loaded("main") # FALSE
dyn.load("blocker.so")
q(save = "no")

Ostensibly at this point, I could do

.Call("main")

and it would run the blocker model, except at the moment we have no way to pass the data or sampler arguments.

My guess is that demo/gm will ultimately need some sort of argument or flag that to tell it whether to generate code in "stand alone mode" or "R mode" or something like that.

So what we did the other day with inline probably would have worked fine if we had managed to first set

export PKG_CXXFLAGS="-I/opt/stan/src -I/opt/stan/lib -std=c++0x"

before calling cxxfunction()

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] matrix vector multiplication with diag_matrix
messages.body_plain:
This discussion should also probably be on
stan-users, not that it's had any traffic yet.

I really need to write some doc!  And work on some
better parser error messages.

The basic problem is that Stan's not very sophisticated
about the syntax for matrices.  All the operations need
to be spelled out Lisp-like (I plan to add better parsing
for them at some point).

The expression for matrix product is "multiply(x,y)".
You can see the available ops in src/stan/math/matrix.hpp and
src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp.

 > lambda[t] ~ multi_normal( diag_matrix(1-phi)*mu +
 > diag_matrix(phi)*lambda[t-1], U );
 >
 > where lambda, phi and mu are vectors and U is a cov_matrix.

To get (phi - 1), you need to either create a unit
vector one and use "minus(phi,one)", or write it
out longhand (which is just as fast as everything's
automatically "vectorized" when the generated code gets
compiled).  For instance, you can do phi-1 this way if
phi is a parameter:

transformed parameters {
    vector(K) phi_m_1;  // K should be sample size
    for (k in 1:K)  phi_m_1[k] <- phi[k] - 1;

}

messages.body_plain:
No, we're not trying to be consistent with BUGS
or with JAGS (which aren't themselves consistent
with each other).

Our variables are typed.  We have many more special
fucntions.  We don't have the same parameterizations
of densities.  We allow improper priors.  We allow
direct manipulation of the total log probability
function so you can define your own densities or
transformations of existing densities (with Jacobian
determinants).

To be consistent with JAGS, we'd also need to use the funky
"%*%" notation for matrix operators, whereas I'm just
going to overload "*", etc.

We're behind in not having all the cumulative
densities (yet) and not having all the random generation
functions (again, as of yet).  Those, we plan to add
as we go along.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] matrix vector multiplication with diag_matrix

I agree that whatever convention we use needs to be able to
distinguish between elementwise multiplication and inner products, and
also that we should adopt some existing convention for that. As a
Matlab user, I find R's %*% notation a little obnoxious (it smells
like something that someone who doesn't do much matrix multiplication
might invent), but if we anticipate having more R users than Matlab
users then it might make sense to use that. Then there's Python's
approach, which is to do matrix multiplication using the dot()
function. Which is also a little ridiculous, but only because "dot()"
isn't a very accurate name.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Maybe we can call our currently function syntax
Python-like (or is that really numpy-like?)
and be done with it.

Seriously, though, I haven't at all been concerned
with compatibility with anything existing.  I've tried to
be internally consistent, but we could use some review.

I went with full versions of distribution names,
like normal(0,1), instead of norm(0,1) or R/BUGS/JAGS
dnorm(0,1).   And our parameterization uses scale, not
precision or squared scale.

I suppose we could add a precision-parameterized

     normal(mu,tau)

and then add a scale-parameterized version,

    normal_scale(mu,sigma);

and one with squared scale (aka variance), as in:

    normal_squared_scale(mu,sigma_sq);

We also have the Cholesky-factor parameterization in the
multivariate case.

There are no element-wise ops, at least not yet.  I've
reduced results where possible.  So there are ops like:

   double multiply(row_vector,vector);

   matrix multiply(vector,row_vector);

But there are NO element-wise ops like:

   vector multiply(vector,vector);

Should we add elementwise ops?  And what should they be
called?

Does JAGS have element-wise ops?  If I do (v1 * v2),
is that interpreted element-wise?  Is that why they use the
funny %*% notation for matrix ops?  I didn't see it in their
doc (I could've missed it or it could just not be in the doc).

I haven't implemented dim(matrix), so no:

    vector<int> dim(matrix);

On the other hand, there are generic dot products,

   double dot_product(vector,vector);
   double dot_product(row_vector,vector);

but I spelled the name out in full.

We're also not allowing the left-hand-side assignment
algebra, as in:

    logit(theta) <- x

and instead require:

    theta <- inv_logit(x)

We just have to make up our minds before I start the doc
process.

- Bob

messages.subject: matrix operation notation
messages.body_plain:
I don't think we need to do this right away,
but eventually, it'd be nice to expand
our existing functional syntax to matrix
operators.

MATLAB looks nicer than R/BUGS/JAGS for matrix
operation syntax, because the basic arithmetic
ops have their natural translation to corresponding
matrix ops.

   A * B    matrix multiply
   A .* B   elementwise multiply

   A ./ B   elementwise divide

   A + B    matrix and elementwise add

   A - B    matrix and elementwise subtract

   +A       matrix positive (no op)

   -A       matrix negation

   A ^ n    matrix power

   A .^ B   elementwise power

The only thing I don't like is:

   A'       complex conjugate transpose

   A.'      transpose

But I suppose we can write A' since it has the same
behavior as A' for real-valued matrices.  Matt -- what's
the convention in MATLAB -- do people just write A'
for real matrix transposes, too?

This brings up the issue of logical operations on
matrices like (A && B) and any(A).  We don't really have
booleans yet, but if we add conditionals (which I think
we eventually should), then we'll need boolean types, and
then it'll make sense to have logical operations.

Anyway, let's not turn this into a bikeshed issue.  There's
apparently even a name for bikeshedding on programming
language syntax, namely "Wadler's Law".  See:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_Law_of_Triviality

Andrew:  this topic looks ripe for blogging.  You've mentioned
Parkinson's First Law, but not his Law of Triviality as far
as I could search.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan has matrix operator syntax
messages.body_plain:
Done.  We now have, in groups of descending
precedence:

   ---------------------------
   A'       transpose
   ---------------------------
   -A       negate
   ---------------------------
   A * B    product
   A .* B   element-wise product
   A ./ B   element-wise division
   ---------------------------
   A + B    sum
   A - B    difference
   ---------------------------

This includes all types that are appropriate.  The
result is the minimal type that can be inferred from
the type of the arguments.

So you can write multivariate expressions like:

    (mu - y)' * Sigma * (mu - y)

and

     sigma * Omega * sigma'

I'm going to doc this on an op-by-op basis.  Product's
the worst:

    (real * real)         : real
    (real * vector)       : vector
    (real * row_vector)   : row_vector
    (real * matrix)       : matrix

    (vector * real)       : vector
    (vector * row_vector) : matrix

    (row_vector * real)   : row_vector
    (row_vector * vector) : real
    (row_vector * matrix) : row_vector

    (matrix * real)       : matrix
    (matrix * vector)     : vector
    (matrix * matrix)     : matrix

And remember that int values are promoted to real where
necessary.

We'll catch as syntax errors, things like (matrix * row_vector).
Even though the sizes are dynamic and not type checked, we
don't allow this operation even if the matrix is (N x 1).

The only other op that seems reasonable to add is
power:

    (real ^ real)         : real    (pow)

and matrix power:

    (matrix ^ int)        : matrix  (matrix power)

and elementwise powers:

    (matrix .^ real)      : matrix
    (vector .^ real)      : vector
    (row_vector .^ real)  : row_vector

which has higher precedence than product.

No one seems to use an operator for inverse, but we
probably want to discourage it in favor of more
stable alternatives.

- Bob

P.S.  Math terminology quiz: Product is to multiplication
       as ??? is to division?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan has matrix operator syntax
messages.body_plain:
On 3/6/12 2:32 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> On Tue, Mar 6, 2012 at 1:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com
> <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>     Done.  We now have, in groups of descending
>     precedence:
>
>
> Awesome!  That should make my models much more readable. :)
>
>     We'll catch as syntax errors, things like (matrix * row_vector).
>     Even though the sizes are dynamic and not type checked, we
>     don't allow this operation even if the matrix is (N x 1).
>
>
> Any reason in particular for this?  While it seems like an unusual use
> case, it is potentially valid.

The main reason is to catch type errors in the programs
at compile time rather than run time.

The Eigen types implementing the basic types are:

    vector_d       ==>  Eigen<double,Dynamic,1>
    row_vector_d   ==>  Eigen<double,1,Dynamic>
    matrix_d       ==>  Eigen<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>

with vector_v, row_vector_v, and matrix_v being the
same with double replaced by stan::agrad::var auto-dif
variables (Stan figures out which to use on a case-by-case
basis at compile time.)

Because Eigen specializes the class template for the
situation where one of the dimensions is 1, these are
really different types and behave differently (though
implement many of the same concepts, including matrix).

Eigen allows you to use a vector like a matrix, but
not vice versa, even if it has vector dimensions.
So if you declare a matrix variable

   Eigen<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> v(5,1);

even though you have a (5 x 1) matrix, aka a vector, it
doesn't support vector operations like dot product that
are built into the specialized vector types.

I could allow the same thing as Eigen, and keep the one
way "vectors may be used as matrices, but not vice-versa",
but I thought it'd be cleaner just to fully separate
the types here.  I think that makes more sense for the kind
of models we foresee people building.

Having said that, we could support lifting of vectors
to matrices:

    to_matrix(vector)      : matrix
    to_matrix(row_vector)  : matrix

which would always work.  The other way around could
throw runtime errors if the dimensions are wrong:

    to_vector(matrix)      : vector
    to_row_vector(matrix)  : row_vector

When in doubt, I tend to go with "don't include it" and
"be strict in the syntax".

>     No one seems to use an operator for inverse, but we
>     probably want to discourage it in favor of more
>     stable alternatives.
>
>
> Matlab uses \ and / to denote the solution of linear systems, i.e., x =
> A\b.  It helps to discourage people doing things like x = inv(A)*b.

Cool.  That'd be easy to add and potentially useful.

Is the operation left associative at the same precedence
as multiplication.

    a / b * c  == (a / b) * c

    a * b / c  == (a * b) / c

That is, do we have:

    A \ b * C  == (A \ b) * C

    C * A \ b  == (C * A) \ b

Does anyone ever use the rightward version?

    b / A == b * inv(A)

and does it have the precednece I'd expect

    C * b / A == (C * b) / A

    b / A * C == (b / A) * C

This is bringing back my algebra days -- I used left and
right residuals in the string semigroup for models of natural
language syntax (categorial grammars based on some algebraic
work of Lambek in the 1950s).  I didn't realize they were
used for matrices.

>     P.S.  Math terminology quiz: Product is to multiplication
>           as ??? is to division?
>
>
> Quotient?

Thanks.  I couldn't think of that word for the life of me.

And more seriously, thanks for the technical input.

- Bob

Will do.  I think it'll be neatest to have two
packages in R.

1.  epilogue
This is our Coda replacement.  No dependency
on rstan.

2.  rstan
This has the stan() function, which returns
an epilogue object.  Dependency on epilogue.

My question is whether we code the epilogue functionality
in C++ or in R?  The former makes it more portable to
other integrations and also usable from the Stan-C++ lib.
The latter is simpler and easier for other people to use
and also easier to install in R (though the C++ shouldn't
be too painful as we need to get R sorted with respect
to the Stan C++ lib in order to write rstan).

I chose "epilogue" because it's a synonym of "coda",
and "rstan" because it's apparently the convention
(though case is all over the place (R2jags, rjags,
Rcpp, R2WinBUGS, ...).  I'm happy to call them whatever
everyone thinks is best.  We'll be lucky if our stan
falls in the top 100 hits for the Google search [stan].
BUGS is on page 4 for [bugs], which is pretty good,
so there's some hope!

messages.subject: contributed model repository
messages.body_plain:
On 3/4/12 10:43 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
 > Hi Bob.  We should be collecting a list of examples that can't be fit
 > in Bugs, Jags, etc.  Here's an example that might be worth looking
 > into, ...

I'd like to get some mechanism for users to contribute
models, data, and short writeups (like the BUGS examples).

Do we want to vet them?  I don't want to start the implicit
journal of Stan models and wind up with tons of editorial
and model-implementation work.  But then I don't want any old
thing to get thrown into the example bin.  Any ideas?

I took a quick look at the paper behind the example Andrew
was talking about:

   Lockwood, J.R. et al. 2007.  Bayesian methods
   for scalable multivariate value-added assessment.
   J. Ed. and Behav. Stat.

The authors say:

---------------
We implemented this model in WinBUGS (Spiegelhalter, Thomas, & Best,
1999), free software for Bayesian model fitting available at
http://www.mrc-bsu .cam.ac.uk/bugs/welcome.shtml <http://cam.ac.uk/bugs/welcome.shtml>. The WinBUGS
implementation was sufficiently fast to estimate the variable
persistence model with small data sets and the com- plete persistence
model with small or large data sets. However, fitting the vari- able
persistence model with large data sets or multiple subjects was
prohibitively slow. Therefore, we developed an MCMC algorithm (specified
in detail in the appendix) for sampling the posterior distribution and
programmed it in C, re- sulting in an efficient and scalable
implementation of the multisubject variable persistence model. We use
this algorithm for all results reported in this article.
---------------

The appendix has their own sampler, which works on the residuals
in the GLM setting (is this what the GLM module of JAGS does -- I
thought that was more about aggregating the sufficieint statistics).

This example is a nice example of what we'd like Stan to be able
to handle out of the box.  But we don't do anything clever for
sparsity (yet, anyway).

- Bob

On 3/7/12 3:26 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
 > So I implemented subtraction by a scalar in stan.  I've attached a
 > patch.

Thanks for the code and heads up about the misnamed
divide operator.  Yes, it's very close to the conventions
we've used.

We can add you (Marcus) as a committer to the Stan project
so this doesn't all have to go through e-mails.  How do
you feel about doc and unit tests?  You can find the tests
under stan/test -- we're using the googletest framework, which
is like JUnit for Java.

?? for EVERYONE:
-----------------
As to this specific patch (and presumably its sibling,
addition by scalar), what does everyone else think about
having this kind of broadcasting of constants up to
appropriately sized vectors or matrices?  With v a vector,
m a matrix, and c a scalar, this would be:

   vector:  (v - c)(i) = v(i) - c

   matrix:  (m - c)(i,j) = m(i,j) - c

Is this something that's done in MATLAB?  In standard
vector notation?

I also have some (long) comments on efficiency and some of
the standards we've tried to follow.  Your implementation (for
matrices) is:

     inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double& c) {
       matrix_d c_(m.rows(),m.cols());
       c_.fill(c);
       return m - c_;
     }

I'm wondering if it'd be more efficient to do this explicitly:

     inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double c) {
         matrix_d mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
         for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
             mc(i) = m(i) - c;
         return mc;
     }

This unfortunately relies on fixed row-major or column-major
ordering because it uses unary accessors.

But then your last line, "return m - c_;" should be using
a template expression for (m - c_) rather than allocating, so
the return-by-value should copy directly without creating
an intermediate in situations like:

      matrix_d mc = m - c;

So they're probably very similar in terms of performance, with
the only difference being the second loop through the data
done by fill(c).

?? for BEN:
-----------
What we'd really like is a no-allocation template expression
for a constant M x N matrix (like your "c_"), but I can't figure
out how to do that in Eigen (CwiseNullaryOp, as returned
by Constant() looks promising).  Ben?

You can use size() on matrices and it gives you rows * cols.
This is potentially unsafe if m doesn't have the default
row-major/col-major setting.  We've just stuck with the col-major
defaults, so it'll be OK as called from Stan, but not as a general
API function.  A full double loop is safer, but much less efficient
in that there's all the index arithmetic

     for (int j = 0; j < c.cols(); ++j)
         for (int i = 0; i < c.rows(); ++i)
             mc(i,j) = m(i,j) - c

We stuck with Eigen's col-major default, so
the loop should at least be col-major.

We relaly want that constant template expression.

We've saved the "x_" style of variables for class member variables
to separate them visually from local variables (we've also been
inconsistent and used "_x" and I used "x__" inside of models to
avoid name clashes with Stan variables).

I haven't profiled, but every piece of advice I've ever
seen says that doubles should be passed by value where
possible.  There are some clever ways to template out an arg
so that it's by value for primitives and otherwise by ref --
Alexandrescu discusses this in his C++ book and the approach
is implemented more or less in Boost.  But we haven't gone that
far down the optimization path, yet.  I'd rather get things
working before getting too carried away on optimization (despite
how I may sound in this e-mail).

We don't want to promote a matrix or vector of scalars to
an auto dif variable (using to_var()) unless we have to,
as the creation of auto-dif variables is expensive.
I plan to go back in and optimize all the vector ops to
avoid many of the to_var() that are there and also partially
evaluate the auto-difs as we've already done for the basic
functions.

The code's essentially the same:

     template <typename T1, typename T2>
     inline Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic>
     subtract(const Matrix<T1,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m,
              const T2& c) {
         Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic> mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
         for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
             mc(i) = m(i) - c;
         return mc;
     }

A single templated function could work for all four cases
of double/var for T1 and T2:

     template <typename T1, typename T2>
     inline Matrix<typename promote_args<T1,T2>::type,Dynamic,Dynamic>
     subtract(const Matrix<T1,Dynamic,Dynamic>& m,
              const T2& c) {
         Matrix<typename promote_args<T1,T2>::type,Dynamic,Dynamic>
             mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
         for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
             mc(i) = m(i) - c;
         return mc;
     }

In fact, if you pull out the two Dynamic template params and replace
them with template params, you could generalize across vectors,
row vectors and matrices, too -- they all support size() and
unary operator() for references.

But as you saw, I've broken these down into separate functions
because all the auto-dif stuff needs a round of unfolding
for optimization (as we've done with the basic functions
you see in stan/agrad/agrad.hpp).  And the doc's also a lot
easier than the mess of promotions above.

Also, I've been un-inlining anything that has loops like this.
In general, we only want to inline fairly short programs.  Of
course, the compiler probably won't inline the big ones anyway -- it's
only a suggestion.

- Bob

This is MATLAB's convention and to me it is relatively unambiguous and allows for reasonable optimization.  The other ways to handle the functionality that I've seen include:

1) require users to define extra "transformed parameters" which manually build vectors and matrices full of the constant
2) provide a ones() function or something similar which produces a matrix (or vector) of appropriate size which can then be multiplied by the desired constant
3) interpret +/- constants as operating on each element of a matrix/vector (what I implemented)

(1) is cumbersome and potentially leads to excess memory usage, although it would be reasonably fast in terms of computation.  (2) is the slowest of the options, providing little ability to optimize the code as the intention of the user is hard to discern.  That said, functions like ones() and eye() (for identity matrices) are generally handy to have.  So I went with (3) since it allows for relatively efficient implementation if done properly (what I did probably isn't).

> So they're probably very similar in terms of performance, with

Assuming Eigen/the compiler is smart, I would think fill() for basic numeric types would reduce to a memset() call which is itself notably faster than looping and repeatedly indexing.  I could certainly be wrong.

> We've saved the "x_" style of variables for class member variables

In retrospect that's probably true for 64bit machines.  On 32bit machines I'd always been told that it's faster to pass by reference since it's half the amount data getting pushed onto the stack.  For inlined function it's largely irrelevant, so long as the function doesn't modify the value of the double.

> But we haven't gone that
> far down the optimization path, yet.  I'd rather get things

Fair enough.  That said I've always found it worth thinking about throughout.  Design decisions made now can have performance impacts that could be hard or tedious to fix later.

> for optimization (as we've done with the basic functions
> you see in stan/agrad/agrad.hpp).  And the doc's also a lot
> easier than the mess of promotions above.

I'm not sure I follow you in terms of the docs.  Having dozens of "add" functions compared to one seems more confusing to me or am I missing your meaning?

> Also, I've been un-inlining anything that has loops like this.
> In general, we only want to inline fairly short programs.  Of
> course, the compiler probably won't inline the big ones anyway -- it's
> only a suggestion.

Yeah, I've generally understood inline to be more about allowing the compiler to inline it if it chooses to, rather than forcing it to do anything.  My only argument for keeping those inlined is that ideally most of those loops would eventually go away and be replaced by modular calls to other appropriate functions and at that point someone would need to remember to add the inline designation back in.

Cheers,
Marcus

>     On 3/7/12 3:26 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>      > So I implemented subtraction by a scalar in stan.  I've attached a
>      > patch.
>

>     we've used.
>

>     you feel about doc and unit tests?  You can find the tests
>     under stan/test -- we're using the googletest framework, which
>     is like JUnit for Java.
>
>
> I would be happy to contribute to the doc and unit tests as needed.  I'm
> a bit rusty on my software engineering skills though and have never used
> either JUnit or googletest so I would ask for you patience.  The last
> serious software engineering (in contrast to research hacking) I've done
> was probably 10 years ago.  I believe JUnit might have just been
> introduced at the time but maybe not...

JUnit was definitely around ten years ago.  But the concept's
older.  The framework's pretty simple if you look at the tests
and Daniel has everything instrumented so you can just run tests
by:

% cd $STAN
% make test/math/matrix

The test itself is in $STAN/src/test/math/matrix_test.cpp.

There's a matching test in test/agrad/matrix for the auto-dif
stuff.

>     ?? for EVERYONE:
>     -----------------
>     As to this specific patch (and presumably its sibling,
>     addition by scalar), what does everyone else think about
>     having this kind of broadcasting of constants up to
>     appropriately sized vectors or matrices?  With v a vector,
>     m a matrix, and c a scalar, this would be:
>
>       vector:  (v - c)(i) = v(i) - c
>
>       matrix:  (m - c)(i,j) = m(i,j) - c
>
>     Is this something that's done in MATLAB?  In standard
>     vector notation?
>
>
>
> This is MATLAB's convention and to me it is relatively unambiguous and
> allows for reasonable optimization.

I don't see any problem with ambiguity.  And it'll definitely
be the most optimizable approach.

> The other ways to handle the
> functionality that I've seen include:
>
> 1) require users to define extra "transformed parameters" which manually
> build vectors and matrices full of the constant
> 2) provide a ones() function or something similar which produces a
> matrix (or vector) of appropriate size which can then be multiplied by
> the desired constant
> 3) interpret +/- constants as operating on each element of a
> matrix/vector (what I implemented)
>
> (1) is cumbersome and potentially leads to excess memory usage, although
> it would be reasonably fast in terms of computation.

Actually, (1) is independent of (2) and (3).  We could construct
ahead the templated constant and re-use it, which would be even
more efficient than building it each time (though probably close, it's
a very simple function).

(3) is definitely what we want, but I we'll get it through
template expressions.  At which point we can optimize further
by pre-building the template expression as in (1).

If we have a const(M,N,x) function, we can expose (2) and get
the efficiency of (3).  That's the beauty of template expressions.

> (2) is the slowest
> of the options, providing little ability to optimize the code as the
> intention of the user is hard to discern.  That said, functions like
> ones() and eye() (for identity matrices) are generally handy to have.

I don't think I could bear the name "eye()".  Tell me they don't
use that in MATLAB.  Please.  People used "liszt" in Prolog because
"list" was reserved, and it drove me bonkers.  They use "clazz" in
Java because "class" is reserved.

You couldn't have a ones() function as is, it'd have to be ones(M,N)
with the sizes.  This is actually what Eigen does, though I now see
they implement it efficiently storing only the sizes and value.

> So I went with (3) since it allows for relatively efficient
> implementation if done properly (what I did probably isn't).

The best implementation would be to have a very small on-the-stack
template expression, and it turns out that's what Eigen does (see
below).

>     I also have some (long) comments on efficiency and some of
>     the standards we've tried to follow.  Your implementation (for
>     matrices) is:
>
>         inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double& c) {
>           matrix_d c_(m.rows(),m.cols());
>           c_.fill(c);
>           return m - c_;
>         }
>
>     I'm wondering if it'd be more efficient to do this explicitly:
>
>         inline matrix_d subtract(const matrix_d& m, const double c) {
>             matrix_d mc(m.rows(),m.cols());
>             for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
>                 mc(i) = m(i) - c;
>             return mc;
>         }
>
>     This unfortunately relies on fixed row-major or column-major
>     ordering because it uses unary accessors.
>
>     But then your last line, "return m - c_;" should be using
>     a template expression for (m - c_) rather than allocating, so
>     the return-by-value should copy directly without creating
>     an intermediate in situations like:
>
>          matrix_d mc = m - c;
>
>     So they're probably very similar in terms of performance, with
>     the only difference being the second loop through the data
>     done by fill(c).
>
>
> Assuming Eigen/the compiler is smart, I would think fill() for basic
> numeric types would reduce to a memset() call which is itself notably
> faster than looping and repeatedly indexing.  I could certainly be wrong.

I finally bit the bullet and tracked down what was
going on in Eigen (I was more curious than concerned about
the case we're looking at).

Your intuitions are right, but for the wrong reason.

fill() is just an alias for setConstant, which does this
(from CwiseNullaryOp.h in Eigen/Core):

template<typename Derived>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE Derived&
PlainObjectBase<Derived>::setConstant(Index rows, Index cols, const
Scalar& value)
{
   resize(rows, cols);
   return setConstant(value);
}

which calls this:

template<typename Derived>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE Derived& DenseBase<Derived>::setConstant(const
Scalar& value)
{
   return derived() = Constant(rows(), cols(), value);
}

The derived() thing is from their use of the so-called curiously
recurring template pattern.  This then calls this method:

template<typename Derived>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE const typename DenseBase<Derived>::ConstantReturnType
DenseBase<Derived>::Constant(Index rows, Index cols, const Scalar& value)
{
   return DenseBase<Derived>::NullaryExpr(rows, cols,
internal::scalar_constant_op<Scalar>(value));
}

which then calls:

template<typename Derived>
template<typename CustomNullaryOp>
EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE const CwiseNullaryOp<CustomNullaryOp, Derived>
DenseBase<Derived>::NullaryExpr(Index rows, Index cols, const
CustomNullaryOp& func)
{
   return CwiseNullaryOp<CustomNullaryOp, Derived>(rows, cols, func);
}

and finally, we construct the CwiseNullaryOp, which only stores the
number of rows, number of columns, and the functor (which is just
a single value promoted in the second to last call above).

>     ?? for BEN:
>     -----------
>     What we'd really like is a no-allocation template expression
>     for a constant M x N matrix (like your "c_"), but I can't figure

Ben liked the array() thingy too.  I can look into playing
nicely with vectors.

>

I think that's more our inconsistency.

>     I haven't profiled, but every piece of advice I've ever
>     seen says that doubles should be passed by value where
>     possible.  There are some clever ways to template out an arg
>     so that it's by value for primitives and otherwise by ref --
>     Alexandrescu discusses this in his C++ book and the approach
>     is implemented more or less in Boost.
>
>
> In retrospect that's probably true for 64bit machines.  On 32bit
> machines I'd always been told that it's faster to pass by reference
> since it's half the amount data getting pushed onto the stack.  For
> inlined function it's largely irrelevant, so long as the function
> doesn't modify the value of the double.

That's the general advice for both 32-bit and 64-bit situations.
It will probably depend on how the variable gets used in the function,
but the problem with refs is that you need to chase pointers, then
bring the 64 bits into registers.  This is going to be
way more expensive than copying an extra 32 bits in terms
of memory non-locality, which is the main killer given how much
faster CPUs are than memory these days.

Even some structs, like our var, could probably be as efficiently,
if not more efficiently, passed by value.  They're just pointers
to implementation, so they're only 8 bytes.

Again, this is something we can play with later.

>     But we haven't gone that
>     far down the optimization path, yet.  I'd rather get things
>     working before getting too carried away on optimization (despite
>     how I may sound in this e-mail).
>
>
> Fair enough.  That said I've always found it worth thinking about
> throughout.  Design decisions made now can have performance impacts that
> could be hard or tedious to fix later.

I agree.  The issue for me is that they need to be designed
so that they can be optimized later.  In that sense, we can
add (v - c), and worry about how to implement it more efficiently
later without changing the modeling language.  That's all I'm
really worried about now.

>     We don't want to promote a matrix or vector of scalars to
>     an auto dif variable (using to_var()) unless we have to,
>     as the creation of auto-dif variables is expensive.
>     I plan to go back in and optimize all the vector ops to

>     evaluate the auto-difs as we've already done for the basic
>     functions.
>
>
> I'll try to go back and rework what I've done in those terms.
>
>     But as you saw, I've broken these down into separate functions
>     because all the auto-dif stuff needs a round of unfolding
>     for optimization (as we've done with the basic functions
>     you see in stan/agrad/agrad.hpp).  And the doc's also a lot
>     easier than the mess of promotions above.
>
>
> I'm not sure I follow you in terms of the docs.  Having dozens of "add"
> functions compared to one seems more confusing to me or am I missing
> your meaning?

It's that each one has simpler doc that doesn't involve
calculated return types.

But I doubt anyone's going to use the doxygen doc anyway.
It's almost useless for Boost and Eigen in my experience,
given their insane levels of complexity.

>     Also, I've been un-inlining anything that has loops like this.
>     In general, we only want to inline fairly short programs.  Of
>     course, the compiler probably won't inline the big ones anyway -- it's
>     only a suggestion.
>
>
> Yeah, I've generally understood inline to be more about allowing the
> compiler to inline it if it chooses to, rather than forcing it to do
> anything.  My only argument for keeping those inlined is that ideally
> most of those loops would eventually go away and be replaced by modular
> calls to other appropriate functions and at that point someone would
> need to remember to add the inline designation back in.

Either way, we'll profile when we want to do the next
speed improvements, and that'll tell us where the
hot spots are in practice.

- Bob

R has diag() and Diag().  diag() takes a vector as input and creates a diagonal matrix.  If you give diag a single scalar it creates a matrix, i.e, diag(5) is the same as diag(rep(1,5)).  Diag() takes a square matrix as input and outputs the vector of diagonals.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] contributed model repository
messages.body_plain:
I don't know about the big repository, I agree that (a) it would be good to have a Stan list like the Bugs list where people can help each other, and (b) I don't want to be vetting this.  One approach would be to have some sort of standard format (analogous to the requirments for an R package) so that models could be checked automatically.  Not a priority, though.

What I was more immediately thinking about was a set of examples for the papers and grant submissions, examples of real problems that Stan can solve but other approaches could not easily solve.

The hope with Lockwood's example is that it would run ok in Stan, either straight out of the box or if necessary with some customized code (which would then be there for future stan models)

A

On Mar 7, 2012, at 1:33 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On 3/4/12 10:43 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Hi Bob.  We should be collecting a list of examples that can't be fit
> > in Bugs, Jags, etc.  Here's an example that might be worth looking
> > into, ...
>
> I'd like to get some mechanism for users to contribute
> models, data, and short writeups (like the BUGS examples).
>
> Do we want to vet them?  I don't want to start the implicit
> journal of Stan models and wind up with tons of editorial
> and model-implementation work.  But then I don't want any old
> thing to get thrown into the example bin.  Any ideas?
>
> I took a quick look at the paper behind the example Andrew
> was talking about:
>
>  Lockwood, J.R. et al. 2007.  Bayesian methods
>  for scalable multivariate value-added assessment.
>  J. Ed. and Behav. Stat.
>
> The authors say:
>
> ---------------
> We implemented this model in WinBUGS (Spiegelhalter, Thomas, & Best, 1999), free software for Bayesian model fitting available at http://www.mrc-bsu .cam.ac.uk/bugs/welcome.shtml <http://cam.ac.uk/bugs/welcome.shtml>. The WinBUGS implementation was sufficiently fast to estimate the variable persistence model with small data sets and the com- plete persistence model with small or large data sets. However, fitting the vari- able persistence model with large data sets or multiple subjects was prohibitively slow. Therefore, we developed an MCMC algorithm (specified in detail in the appendix) for sampling the posterior distribution and programmed it in C, re- sulting in an efficient and scalable implementation of the multisubject variable persistence model. We use this algorithm for all results reported in this article.
> ---------------
>
> The appendix has their own sampler, which works on the residuals
> in the GLM setting (is this what the GLM module of JAGS does -- I
> thought that was more about aggregating the sufficieint statistics).
>
> This example is a nice example of what we'd like Stan to be able
> to handle out of the box.  But we don't do anything clever for
> sparsity (yet, anyway).

The problem is that we're really thinking of the C++ lib
as having 0-based indexing.  The Stan code generator
does all the subtraction of 1 to get the MATLAB/BUGS/R-style
indexing from 1.  Except for the row() and col() functions.
So what we really need is some other row() and col() functions.

So I'dd add row0() and col0() methods if we really wanted
to fully support 0-based indexing at the API level.

On our previous topic, efficiency concerns are different
in the agrad case than the double case.  Anything that
saves creating new agrad::var instances is going to be a win
over using the clever/small template expressions.  This will
mainly be an issue in the (Matrix<double> * var) methods,
because the promotion of the Matrix<double> to Matrix<var> is
so expensive.  It's faster to just create the Matrix<var>
result directly.

- Bob

The textbookish multi_normal_log() function is a self-inflicted efficiency disaster, and we had planned to change it. The cherry on top is that we already construct L in cov_matrix_constrain() and then post-multiply it by L' to get Sigma (to then decompose three times).

It is better to utilize multi_normal_cholesky_log() if possible.

Ben

Mainly, only the modeling language uses 1-based indexing.
The only places it touches the API is in row() and col().
I was originally thinking I'd need to do something to declare
which arguments of which functions needed a -1 in them,
but it was simpler to just change row() and col() and put
in warnings in the doc.  If we get lots of people wanting to
use our API, we may need to rethink.

Having multiple namespaces is trickier.  I'd rather try to
keep that simpler.  The old-school approach would IFDEF the
-1 with some property.  The new-school approach would be to
add policy template args to everything.  This all seems like
overkill.

The right solution in the longer term is to get rid of the
matrix library altogether in favor of adding
heterogeneous binary ops to Eigen itself (allowing
you to multiply Matrix<A> with Matrix<B> whenever you can
multiply an A by a B, in particular with A=double, B=stan::agrad::var),
we can get rid of our whole matrix lib, which is just there
to wrap stan::agrad::var so that we can use matrix ops.

No matter what we do the gradients are going to be the
biggest part of the computation.  We've got our own arena-based
memory management for the new() calls.  There's a ton of work
being done in the virtual chain methods, but it's either that
or pointers to functions, and either way, it's a deref for
every chaining function call.  There's really no way to do it
all statically -- we need to store different kinds of expressions
on the derivative propagation stack.

Ben's got a bunch of stuff queued up for Cholesky decompositions
for multivariates, so you should definitely run what you want to
do by us -- it might already be done (at least conceptually).

I've been trying to control the feature creep so we can actually
get a working version out the door.

- Bob

This is more or less where the discussion ran out of steam last time. Part of the problem is that Eigen does not have a triangular matrix type or a symmetric matrix type, only triangular and self-adjoint "views" of a full matrix, but Doug Bates among other people is hoping that these get added soon. Bob is somewhat reluctant to add new types to stan. I think Andrew was somewhat reluctant to have default behavior that deviates from what people see in textbooks. I kind of liked the idea of having a covariance matrix class whose attributes included all the stuff that any function might need, such as its Cholesky factor, its inverse, a bunch of flags for validity checks, etc. But that would be inconsistent with Stan's mostly functional orientation. So that will have to get worked out. As it stands now, Stan users will likely gravitate toward multivariate models that are at best slow and at worst wrong.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I fiddled with where the Jacobians were getting
done so we'd get the right answers.  I had reasoned
through them to the point where I thought you were
applying the Jacobians yourself, so I took them out
of the transform arguments.

There may still be mistakes, there.  If so, could
you add unit tests that break before adding the
fixes?

Also, please feel free to refactor all of the
Eigen linear algebra.  I repeat, there's no reason
for my textbook implementations other than ignorance!

And if we can add more tests for the derivatives of
some of these complicated things, even better.

The reason there are std::vector instances all over
is that I was trying to minimize the dependence
on Eigen.  In retrospect, that was probably a mistake.

The copying is also the least of our problems
performance-wise in the context of Stan.  But, if we
want to provide a good external library, then we
have to clean this stuff up.

An interim solution to ease the refactoring would be
to add overloaded versions of the functions for Eigen
vectors and matrices.

For vectors, we can lean on the fact that Eigen column
vectors, Eigen row vectors, and std::vector all
implement the .size(), and operator[](size_t i) concepts
(though actually, Eigen uses operator[](int) and
thus goes against the STL conventions).  Given that,
we could use some fancier templating and
treat the argument/result as a template template (because
we need the item type, too, so need to pull out type
params for both std::vector<T> and T)

Matt's suggestion was to take some of these functions
even lower level with iterator/pointer arguments instead
of array arguments.  That makes more sense if you don't
have to do Eigen operations on them.

The multivariate parameters for densities
are all Eigen vectors and matrices, which is where the
incompatibility comes in.

Within an expression in Eigen, you can efficiently Map
a std::vector<T> as an Eigen vector,
but you can't wrap std::vector<std::vector<T>>.

If we want to keep going on optimizing, the way I implemented
the compiled Stan data structures is inefficient as it
relies on std::vector<std::vector<double>> if you declare

  double x[M,N]

That's wasteful in storage compared to an Eigen Matrix, which just
computes the indexing itself (using the row/col major policy).
But we'd need to generalize to x[M,N,K], and so on, to handle
all of the Stan types.

- Bob

My reluctance to add new data types stems from wanting
to get a stable version of Stan out the door.  If you
look at what's involved in adding a new type, it's fairly
involved, but not impossible.

I like the idea of a covariance matrix class.   Much of
what we were talking about, like caching the Cholesky
factor, could be handled behind the scenes.  As I said before,
it would be more like exposing Eigen's LLT object.

As to speed, I want to emphasize that the best thing
we can do for speed is to partially evaluate all the
gradients in:

      stan/agrad/matrix.hpp

The time for doing these ops dominates everything else,
and everywhere we promote a double to a var, we take
a HUGE hit in performance.  Every time you evaluate

    x * y

and x is a double matrix and y is a var matrix, we
create an entire var matrix needlessly, leading not
just to M x N copies, var constructor calls, but also
the overhead of access when we actually do the multiplication,
which itself spews more copies.  This goes for vectors,
too.

I did it that way not because I didn't know how to do it
better, but because it would take a long time to implement
and test it all done the right way.

The poor choices in linear algebra operators were done out
of ignorance, and I again urge you to fix them.  Or we
can sit down and fix them together.

Meanwhile, we need to write that R interface before we
can make a Stan user out of Andrew.

- Bob

messages.subject: more on optimization
messages.body_plain:
Another thing we can do is vectorize some
of the ops.  When you have a covariance matrix
that's being used for multiple observations,
the hard work only needs to be done once.

It's easy enough to do with simple vector data outcomes,
but harder to do with regression models.  Either
the linear (or whatever) predictor needs to be
calculated into an array before calling a vectorized function,
or you need to do the implementation yourself using
vector/matrix ops (presumably what Ben meant by saying
users would do the wrong thing -- he's right, because
users do all sorts of crazy things, like my very
naive use of Eigen).

- Bob

Yes, the function

    matrix cov_matrix_constrain(vector, lp);

needs to convert an ((N choose 2) + N)-dimensional
vector input, with unconstrained finite floating-point values,
into a positive-definite covariance matrix output and
add the log of the absolute Jacobian determinant of the
transform to lp.  (Presumably there's a measure-zero subspace
of input vectors with non-positive-definite outputs.)

> then
> cov_matrix_constrain() should be responsible for adjusting lp due to
>
> A. mapping of unbounded parameters to canonical partial correlations on
> (-1,1)
> B. mapping of unbounded parameters to positive standard deviations

 > Then, downstream functions would be responsible for adjusting lp due to
 >
 > C. mapping of canonical partial correlations to Pearson correlations
 > D. mapping of Pearson correlations to covariances

    template <typename T>

     Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>
     cov_matrix_constrain(const Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>& x,
                                                    size_t k,
                                                    T& lp) {
       size_t k_choose_2 = (k * (k - 1)) / 2;
       Array<T,Dynamic,1> cpcs(k_choose_2);
       int pos = 0;
       for (size_t i = 0; i < k_choose_2; ++i)

[1]        cpcs[i] = corr_constrain(x[pos++]); // ,lp);

       Array<T,Dynamic,1> sds(k);
       for (size_t i = 0; i < k; ++i)

[2]        sds[i] = positive_constrain(x[pos++]); // ,lp);
       return read_cov_matrix(cpcs, sds, lp);
     }

So if read_cov_matrix() isn't applying the Jacobians for
steps (A) and (B), we need to add the lp back to [1] and [2].

And read_cov_matrix() is going to be responsible for C and D.

> A month or so ago, there was a bug due to me being off-by-one in part D,
> but I think you commented out correct implementations of parts A and B.

I very well could have.

> In any event, inconsistency (with the same inits) between wishart and
> wishart2x2 in basic_distributions is sufficient reason to be concerned,
> right?

Indeed.  Something's wrong somewhere if they're not producing
the same results.  The param that gets printed is the unconstrained
version.  So it's not surprising those are the same.  But the
log prob and gradients should be the same, too.
Missing or duplicating part of the Jacobian is a likely culprit.

- Bob

It's certainly not being checked elsewhere.
We want to catch these indexing errors and throw
exceptions.

>     Also, is there no type promotion hackery that would allow us to take
>     advantage of Eigen's templated stuff like
>
>     ( m1.array() OP m2.array() ).matrix();
>
>     I am guessing not (yet) but life will be so much easier when Eigen
>     implements mixed type ops.
>
>
> That should work for the elt_* functions.  I'm using a similar pattern
> for element-wise exp/log functions.  I'm just finishing adding unit
> tests and will commit that change.

Right -- this stuff's no problem as long as you can
make the types consistent.  But if m1 is double and
m2 is var, it probably won't work.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm happy to use my soapbox as you all see fit.
A

On Mar 10, 2012, at 5:44 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On 3/10/12 4:48 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> Another limitation of the way covariance matrices are handled is that we
>> currently do not have a way for the user to utilize the LKJ approach in
>> an intuitive and computationally efficient way. Granted, there are
>> currently only 4 people in the world who think in terms of the LKJ
>> approach and three of them are L, K, and J. But that is the best way to
>> think about it in the stan context.
>
> If you can convince Andrew of this and get him to
> use his bully pulpit AND we put it in Stan, then I
> think that number will be bigger than 4 before long.
>
> From a user perspective, the LKJ version is pretty
> easy to grasp.  Easier than a scaled Wishart, at least.
>
>> The Wishart-family approach in stan mostly makes sense from a syntax
>> perspective, e.g.:
>
> Right.  Currently, it looks just like BUGS.
> Except that we declare W as a covariance matrix.
>
>> master!stan *> cat src/models/basic_distributions/wishart.stan
>> transformed data {
>> cov_matrix(2) S;
>>
>> for (i in 1:2)
>> for (j in 1:2)
>> S[i,j] <- 0.0;
>>
>> S[1,1] <- 2.0;
>> S[2,2] <- 0.5;
>
> A symmetric matrix data type would be nice.
> Or a diagonal matrix data type for this case.
>
> Also, you shouldn't be using a cov_matrix(2) data
> type in transformed data.  The type is only guaranteed
> for reading in the parameter and not monkeying with it.
> So I turned it off in this context.  This is probably
> going to confuse people.
>
>> }
>> parameters {
>> cov_matrix(2) W;
>> }
>> model {
>> W ~ wishart(4, S);
>> }
>>
>> The user has a Wishart prior and the Wishart prior implies some unnamed
>> but calculatable prior beliefs about the primitive parameters that are
>> transformed behind the scenes in cov_matrix(). That was a bit weird to
>> program in C++, but is not wrong and not exposed to the user anyway.
>
> That was the plan!  Looks like there may be a bug or two,
> but conceptually it should work.
>
>> But I anticipate users will tend to utilize Wishart-family priors on
>> covariance matrices because that is what they are familiar with in the
>> literature, rather than that is what is entailed by their prior beliefs.
>
> Yes indeed.  Andrew's very worried about this kind
> of thing, too.  I don't know if he's onboard with the LKJ
> priors, but convincing him and building this into Stan could
> go a long way toward convincing everyone else.
>
> Now's the time to bend his ear about inclusion of material
> in BDA 3, too :-)
>
>> The LKJ approach allows the user to have a prior over each standard
>> deviation and a joint prior (usually uniform, which is implied when eta
>> == 1.0) over the correlation matrix.
>>
>> transformed data {
>> real mu(2);
>> real(0,) sigma(2);
>> real(0,) eta;
>>
>> mu[1] <- 0.0;
>> mu[2] <- 0.0;
>> sigma[1] <- 1.0;
>> sigma[2] <- 0.5;
>> eta <- 1.0;
>> }
>> parameters {
>> cov_matrix(2) W;
>> }
>> model {
>> W ~ lkj_cov(mu, sigma, eta);
>> }
>>
>> But lkj_cov_log() is hard-coded to impose a lognormal prior on the
>> standard deviations, which seems unnecessarily limiting.
>
> Agreed.
>
>> And there is
>> the aforementioned efficiency nightmare where cov_matrix_constrain()
>> first constructs L so that it can be post-multiplied by L' to get W and
>> then lkj_cov_log() conducts a Cholesky decomposition of W to (re)obtain
>> L and then evaluate the density.
>>
>> To do things the right way, we need a function, perhaps called
>> LKJ_mapping(), that is exposed to the user that takes CPCs and standard
>> deviations and produces L such that W := L * L'. And we need a (trivial)
>> C++ version of lkj_cor_log() that takes CPCs and eta. Then, the .stan
>> file could look something like
>>
>> parameters {
>> real(-1,1) CPCs[K_choose_2];
>> real(0,) SDs[K];
>> }
>> transformed parameters {
>> matrix L(K,K);
>> L <- LKJ_mapping(CPCs, SDs);
>> }
>> model {
>> for(i in 1:K)
>> // some prior on SDs[i]
>>
>> CPCs ~ lkj_cor(1.0);
>>
>> // maybe use L as part of a multinormal likelihood or something
>> }
>
> That looks great.  We don't even need to compute anything
> for lkj_cor(alpha) when alpha = 1.0.
>
> All that we need to do this in Stan are the four instances
> of:
>
>    template <typename T1, typename T2>
>    Matrix<typename promote_args<T1,T2>::type,Dynamic,Dynamic>
>    LKJ_mapping(std::vector<T1> cpcs, std::vector<T2> sds);
>
> and
>
>    typename promote_args<T1,T2>::type
>    lkj_cor(std::vector<T1> cpcs, T2 alpha);
>
> That's for T1 in {double,var} and T2 in {double,var}.
>
> In order to use Eigen vectors instead of std::vector in
> the function, we'd need two new Stan types and declarations
> like:
>
>  parameters {
>     corr_vector(K_choose_2) CPCs;
>     pos_vector(K) sds;
>  }
>
> Or I could try to thread through constraints on vector
> values.  Right now, only non-vectors can have constraints.
>
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: CwiseBinaryOp.h, mixed types & vectorization
messages.body_plain:
If you look at line 109 of

   stan/lib/Eigen/src/Core/CwiseBinaryOp.h

you'll find the macro

   EIGEN_CHECK_BINARY_COMPATIBILITY

which is what's throwing our error:

   YOU_MIXED_DIFFERENT_NUMERIC_TYPES_...

The doc above says you can't mix different types.
But they do have a special case for complex inside
the first EIGEN_STATIC_ASSERT.

When they say "vectorization", I think they're
referring to their fixed size optimizations
and things like GPU optimizations (some of which
only work on 32-bit float, I think).

You can see the template specializations for the product
type in the following file starting at line 119:

  Core/Product.h

For instance, gemm is vectorized floating point operations.
I'm pretty sure this determines the expression template
return type for a product and is responsible for figuring
out whether to actually multiply or use something like
gemm vectorization.  Note that Large=2 and Small=3 are just
enum values separated from 1, and all Dynamic dimensions
are Large given the categorization template metaprogram
up at line 62 of Prouct.h.

This all plays out in

  Core/products/GeneralMatrixMatrix.h

where they actually define the access operators that eventually
resolve the expression templates.

Every time I dive into this stuff I get scared and back off.

- Bob

> only work on 32-bit float, I think).

I believe vectorization probably more aptly refers to SIMD instructions (think SSE or, if your memory is that good, MMX) which work on both 32bit and 64bit platforms with both floats and doubles.  However, they are only relevant for basic numeric instructions and loosing vectorization for the double OP vari cases doesn't really matter at this point.

>
> You can see the template specializations for the product
> type in the following file starting at line 119:
>
>  Core/Product.h
>
> For instance, gemm is vectorized floating point operations.
> I'm pretty sure this determines the expression template
> return type for a product and is responsible for figuring
> out whether to actually multiply or use something like
> gemm vectorization.  Note that Large=2 and Small=3 are just
> enum values separated from 1, and all Dynamic dimensions
> are Large given the categorization template metaprogram
> up at line 62 of Prouct.h.
>
> This all plays out in
>
>  Core/products/GeneralMatrixMatrix.h
>
> where they actually define the access operators that eventually
> resolve the expression templates.
>
> Every time I dive into this stuff I get scared and back off.

It seems like the limiting factor here is really that we're defining a var scalar type and constructing an Eigen::Matrix<var> when Eigen really doesn't support non-basic types (except for complex) for entries.

One way around this is might be to define a matrix variant of the vari class.  E.G., something like:

template<int Rows, int Cols>
class vari_matrix : public chainable {
  const Eigen::Matrix<double,Rows,Cols> val_;
...
}

This would allow for fast (and vectorized) implementations of things like multiply(matrix_d,matrix_v).  However, this seems likely to be a rather large design change and would end up being much messier than if Eigen just allowed (non-vectorized) mixed-type operations.

Cheers,
Marcus

There's also all kinds of parallelism directives tied in on
a platform-specific basis at this low level.

The code's pretty dense to work through.

>
>     You can see the template specializations for the product
>     type in the following file starting at line 119:
>
>       Core/Product.h
>
>     For instance, gemm is vectorized floating point operations.
>     I'm pretty sure this determines the expression template

>     out whether to actually multiply or use something like
>     gemm vectorization.  Note that Large=2 and Small=3 are just
>     enum values separated from 1, and all Dynamic dimensions
>     are Large given the categorization template metaprogram
>     up at line 62 of Prouct.h.
>
>     This all plays out in
>

>       Core/products/__GeneralMatrixMatrix.h

>
>     where they actually define the access operators that eventually
>     resolve the expression templates.
>
>     Every time I dive into this stuff I get scared and back off.
>
>
> It seems like the limiting factor here is really that we're defining a
> var scalar type and constructing an Eigen::Matrix<var> when Eigen really
> doesn't support non-basic types (except for complex) for entries.

Just to be clear.  Eigen's fine with our var type, just
not with mixing var and double types.

> One way around this is might be to define a matrix variant of the vari
> class.  E.G., something like:
>
> template<int Rows, int Cols>
> class vari_matrix : public chainable {
>    const Eigen::Matrix<double,Rows,Cols> val_;
> ...
> }

This is the first thing I tried to design, but no luck.

There are several problems with this specific suggestion.
One, we almost certainly want Rows and Cols to be runtime,
not compile time.   Two, we need a similarly shaped adjoint.
So let's assume we really have this:

   class vari_matrix : public chainable {
       Eigen::matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> val_;
       Eigen::matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> adj_;
   }

Now let's suppose we define the operators to work as we
want, so that we have:

    var& vari_matrix::operator()(int m, int n);

and wrap a var_matrix around it:

   class var_matrix {
       vari_matrix* vmi_;
   }

So when you look at this, you realize maybe we could just template
it all:

   template <typename Val>
   class vari {
      Val val_;
      Val adj_;
   }

   template <typename Val>
   class var {
       vari<Val>* vi_;
   }

We have to construct that var using a new vari given val_(m,n)
and adj_(m,n), which is going to be a real drag.  But this should
really be a reference, so that we could do

    vari_matrix x;
    x(m,n) = y;

I never figured out how to do that without a whole lot of work
on a new kind of var that acts like a view back into the matrix
and remains very inefficient.

Then how do we string together expressions like:

    (x - y) * Sigma * (x - y)'

and make sure that they get evaluated with the proper expression
templates AND propagate the right derivatives?  We'd have to
build up our own expressions, I think.

So what I did is just went with Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic> for
matrices, wrote our own matrix ops, and just punted on expressions.

I wish to continue to emphasize that the savings from partially
evaluating the derivatives in the var-based ops will dwarf any
savings from getting the expression templates working within Eigen.
That only solves one of our problems, and even if we do it, makes
evaluating the derivatives actually harder, as we have to start
specializing Eigen's template expressions for Scalar = var.

The really slow part is the promotion of double to var, but
that can all pretty much be eliminated by just implementing our
own basic matrix ops. The only mixed ops are the very simple
ones.

At that point, we'd basically be leaning on Eigen for the linear
algebra and the basic data types, but not for the basic matrix
operations other than get/set.

> This would allow for fast (and vectorized) implementations of things
> like multiply(matrix_d,matrix_v).  However, this seems likely to be a
> rather large design change and would end up being much messier than if
> Eigen just allowed (non-vectorized) mixed-type operations.

Right.  But how do we get the derivatives?  I think we still have
to write all of the propagation ourselves as extensions of vari_matrix
as we did for other ops by extending vari.

- Bob

>     Val val_;
>     Val adj_;
>  }
>
>  template <typename Val>
>  class var {
>      vari<Val>* vi_;
>  }
>
> We have to construct that var using a new vari given val_(m,n)
> and adj_(m,n), which is going to be a real drag.  But this should
> really be a reference, so that we could do
>
>   vari_matrix x;
>   x(m,n) = y;
>
> I never figured out how to do that without a whole lot of work
> on a new kind of var that acts like a view back into the matrix
> and remains very inefficient.

Ah, a good point.  I hadn't considered the indexing issue.  In essence you would need the matrix to contain references to vari-like structures.

>
> Then how do we string together expressions like:
>
>   (x - y) * Sigma * (x - y)'
>
> and make sure that they get evaluated with the proper expression
> templates AND propagate the right derivatives?  We'd have to
> build up our own expressions, I think.

That's true.  The one advantage that would have is allowing handling things like inverse(A) better by exploiting that dinv(A) = -inv(A) * dA * inv(A) as opposed to pushing them through an LU factorization and similarly for determinant(A)/log_determinant(A).  On the whole, probably not worth the trouble.

>
> I wish to continue to emphasize that the savings from partially
> evaluating the derivatives in the var-based ops will dwarf any
> savings from getting the expression templates working within Eigen.
> That only solves one of our problems, and even if we do it, makes
> evaluating the derivatives actually harder, as we have to start
> specializing Eigen's template expressions for Scalar = var.
>
> The really slow part is the promotion of double to var, but
> that can all pretty much be eliminated by just implementing our
> own basic matrix ops. The only mixed ops are the very simple
> ones.

I think there are two independent motivating factors here, at least from my perspective.  One is performance (e.g., working to avoid unneeded promotion to vars) and the other is simplicity of code (e.g., allowing us to simply write A<var> OP B<double> as opposed to reimplementing every op explicitly).  That getting mixed types working would allow the templated expressions to potentially improve performance is really a bonus.

>
> > This would allow for fast (and vectorized) implementations of things
> > like multiply(matrix_d,matrix_v).  However, this seems likely to be a
> > rather large design change and would end up being much messier than if
> > Eigen just allowed (non-vectorized) mixed-type operations.
>
> Right.  But how do we get the derivatives?  I think we still have
> to write all of the propagation ourselves as extensions of vari_matrix
> as we did for other ops by extending vari.

Yeah, that would likely be necessary.  You might be able to avoid some duplication by treating scalars as 1x1 matrices but it would certainly be a big change and not a priority right now if, as you've alluded to elsewhere, the goal is to get something mostly fully featured out there for people to start using.

Cheers,
Marcus

>
>         template<int Rows, int Cols>
>         class vari_matrix : public chainable {

>            const Eigen::Matrix<double,Rows,__Cols> val_;

>         ...

No, Eigen::Matrix has half a dozen or so template parameters,
the first of which is the type, and the second two of which are
rows and columns, which can either be fixed values or Dynamic.

   matrix_d     : Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>
   vector_d     : Matrix<double,Dynamic,1>
   row_vector_d : Matrix<double,1,Dynamic>

When you provide 1 as a fixed column or row size, Eigen uses a
template specialization to implement all the vector operations
like dot().

>
>        Two, we need a similarly shaped adjoint.
>     So let's assume we really have this:
>
>       class vari_matrix : public chainable {
>           Eigen::matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> val_;
>           Eigen::matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> adj_;
>       }
>
>
>
>

>     want, so that we have:
>

>
>     and wrap a var_matrix around it:
>
>       class var_matrix {

>       }
>
>     So when you look at this, you realize maybe we could just template
>     it all:
>
>       template <typename Val>
>       class vari {
>          Val val_;
>          Val adj_;
>       }
>
>       template <typename Val>
>       class var {
>           vari<Val>* vi_;
>       }
>
>     We have to construct that var using a new vari given val_(m,n)
>     and adj_(m,n), which is going to be a real drag.  But this should
>     really be a reference, so that we could do

>

>     and remains very inefficient.
>

> Ah, a good point.  I hadn't considered the indexing issue.  In essence
> you would need the matrix to contain references to vari-like structures.

We could get away with a templated Val.  But it makes
matrix indexing by row/col very expensive because we'd need
a vari<double> that referenced a position in the matrix.
We could implement the vari<double> view into vari<Matrix>
as an extension of vari with a no-op chain(), but it's very
heavy in terms of alloc, virtual no-op calls during auto-dif,
and access during use.

>
>     Then how do we string together expressions like:
>
>        (x - y) * Sigma * (x - y)'
>
