> things like inverse(A) better by exploiting that dinv(A) = -inv(A) * dA
> * inv(A) as opposed to pushing them through an LU factorization and
> similarly for determinant(A)/log_determinant(A).  On the whole, probably
> not worth the trouble.

We can implement our own expressions.

And it's precisiely the kind of handling of derivatives
that this is going to make very hard.

>     I wish to continue to emphasize that the savings from partially
>     evaluating the derivatives in the var-based ops will dwarf any
>     savings from getting the expression templates working within Eigen.
>     That only solves one of our problems, and even if we do it, makes
>     evaluating the derivatives actually harder, as we have to start
>     specializing Eigen's template expressions for Scalar = var.
>
>     The really slow part is the promotion of double to var, but
>     that can all pretty much be eliminated by just implementing our
>     own basic matrix ops. The only mixed ops are the very simple
>     ones.
>
>
> I think there are two independent motivating factors here, at least from
> my perspective.  One is performance (e.g., working to avoid unneeded
> promotion to vars) and the other is simplicity of code (e.g., allowing
> us to simply write A<var> OP B<double> as opposed to reimplementing
> every op explicitly).  That getting mixed types working would allow the
> templated expressions to potentially improve performance is really a bonus.

I completely agree that the syntax would be nice.

We can get rid of the promotion through better implementations
of multiply(), add(), etc.

The problem is that even if we implement every OP explicitly,
it's not enough.  We have to implement all of the expression
templates created by those ops.  When you multiply matrices in
Eigen, or multiply a scalar by a matrix, or add two matrices,
you get an expression template, not a matrix.  And they're all
different expression templates depending on the op. It's only
when you copy or assign that you get everything written out to
a matrix.  So let's say I implement:

   Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic>
   operator*(Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic>,
             Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>);

Then I can write:

   Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic> A(3,3);
   Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> B(3,3);
   Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic> C(3,3);
   ...
   C = A * B;  // OK

   C = A.transpose() * B; // FAIL

   C = (A * A) * B;  // FAIL

The problem is that A.transpose() is not of type
Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic>, nor is (A * A).  They
each have their own expression template type that's
only related to the base type through the curiously
recursive template pattern.  So you need to keep
implementing for all of these expression teplates.

This is what's going to be required to change Eigen to
support mixed operations internally.

I'm forcing a write to Matrix after every op in Stan's
matrix lib.   So you could use Stan's matrix transpose() to
do

   C = multiply(transpose(A),B);

or

   C = multiply(multiply(A,B),C);

The cost for auto-dif is going to dwarf the savings from
expression templates anyway, which is why I did it this way.

In Stan's own language, you get the expressions back, but
they're implemented with the explicit-copy Stan implementations.

It's not impossible to do both right, but just getting the mixed
ops working is only the beginning.  If they're done like complex,
we'll need way more derivative-specific stuff before they're
more efficient than the non-expression-templated way I have it now
with derivatives pushed through.

>
>         This would allow for fast (and vectorized) implementations of things
>         like multiply(matrix_d,matrix_v).  However, this seems likely to
>         be a
>         rather large design change and would end up being much messier
>         than if
>         Eigen just allowed (non-vectorized) mixed-type operations.
>
>
>     Right.  But how do we get the derivatives?  I think we still have
>     to write all of the propagation ourselves as extensions of vari_matrix
>     as we did for other ops by extending vari.
>
>
>
> Yeah, that would likely be necessary.  You might be able to avoid some
> duplication by treating scalars as 1x1 matrices but it would certainly
> be a big change and not a priority right now if, as you've alluded to
> elsewhere, the goal is to get something mostly fully featured out there
> for people to start using.

But Eigen doesn't implement scalars as 1x1 matrices.  I don't
know if it specializes Matrix<T,1,1> for added efficiency in the
really small case.  Probably.

- Bob

> 1.  replace the two loops in read_cov_L() with:

> In which case I see the 2.0 * log_sds.sum(), but why

It wasn't quite right. The two Jacobians in question here are both diagonal. The first Jacobian is for the transformation from correlations to covariances (of order K choose 2). The derivative of a the i,j covariance with respect to the i,j correlation is sd_i * sd_j, and the product of each K choose 2 pairs of standard deviations goes on the diagonal. So, that log determinant is (K - 1) * log_sds.sum().

The second Jacobian is for the transformation from standard deviations to variances (of order K). The derivative of the ith variance is 2 * sd_i. So, the log determinant is (2.0 * sd).log().sum(), which is K * log(2.0) + sd.log().sum(). So, the correct line (which is in the code now) is

log_prob += (sds.log().sum() + log(2.0)) * K;

> 2.  Add the Jacobians back in for the cov_matrix_constrain()

Yes, that was necessary.

messages.subject: Optimization of stack_alloc::alloc
messages.body_plain:
I made some small changes to stack_alloc::alloc() which cut it's cost by ~37%.  Since it's a pretty central function I wanted to run the patch by people before I pushed it.  I've run make test-unit which comes up clean, but I wanted to be doubly sure.

On a related note it seems like (at least in my case) it's not (entirely) extra calls to to_var() that are the culprit.  In fact ~60% of the calls are coming from operators (* and +) being used in Eigen::internal::gebp_kernel which is called by Eigen::internal::general_matrix_matrix_product (from multiply(matrix_v,matrix_v)) and Eigen::internal::triangular_solve_matrix (from multi_normal_cholesky_log).

(For reference, this profiling is done with g++ -O3 using callgrind and the excellent Kcachegrind to visualize results.)

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Awesome.  I'll take a look.  If all of our
unit tests are passing, we should be OK.

g++ -O3 is exactly what we're targeting.  Thanks
for pointing out which tools you used.

I'll take a look and hopefully learn more about C++
optimization.

The other thing to look at is the way objects
get constructed in var and vari -- that's where
the stack allocation's getting called.

For to_var(), I was talking about arithmetic operators of mixed
types, as in Matrix<var> * Matrix<double> and even more so
Matrix<var> + Matrix<double>.  The extra memory overhead hurts
as much as the time.

The solvers shouldn't need to_var() at all, as they work on a single
type.  And we of course expect the solving to dominate (like
the log gamma and digamma functions implicated in some of
the gradients and to a lesser extent, log and exp itself).

For some operations, we know there's no effect on gradients,
like transpose.  But for others like products or sums,
it'd be nice to compute the gradients directly.  That's only
going to help for the solvers if we can push it through to
the operator*() for Eigen matrices used by the solvers.

In some cases (like inverse as you pointed out before),
we might be able to get some speedup by sending a Matrix<double>
to the solver and computing the effect on the gradients ourselves.

- Bob

The typical use pattern for stack_alloc means that eight_byte_aligned_malloc will almost never be called compared to the rest of the code in there.  This is so much the case that eight_byte_aligned_malloc never really shows up on the profiles.

messages.subject: NUTS questions
messages.body_plain:
Two questions about NUTS that (hopefully) should be easy for someone to answer (Matt maybe?).

if you really do need thousands of steps to make any progress then

we only run the algorithm long enough to get, say, a dozen effectively
independent samples, those asymptotic results aren't so relevant.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Wow, a lot happened on the list since earlier
this afternoon!

Marcus -- please feel free to add a parameter to
bound the max number of steps.  It's kosher from
a detailed balance perspective.

The decision we need to make is what to set as
its default value.

Making it too small runs the risk of reverting
to more random-walk-like behavior and therefore
reducing effective sample size.  There's no
risk of periodic cycles due to the U-turn criterion,
so it doesn't technically go into an infinite loop.

Having said that, a default value like 2**20 (1M
or so) seems excessive, whereas 2**8 (256) seems
too small.  I think it should be 2**12 or so.

The problem with making the bound too small is that you
can get more random walk-like behavior without any warning.
Making it too large and it can seem to hang, but at
least you get some feedback that it's having trouble
moving.

Ben's belief is correct -- setting the number of steps
turns off NUTS and reverse to a fixed step-size HMC.  You
can turn on/off step-size adapation (and presumably
mass matrix adaptation when NUTS II is in) independently
of turning on/off NUTS.

Following Radford's advice (in both the MCMC Handbook paper on HMC
and his response to the NUTS paper on his blog), I added the
option to randomize step size (even after adaptation), which is
also kosher for detailed balance.  This can be turned on
independently of NUTS, though Matt doesn't think it'll be necessary
for NUTS.

As to using all the steps of the trajectory, I don't know
how that would play with detailed balance -- you may
need to restrict to samples meeting the slicing criterion.

It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
(from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
is that this should improve the effective sample size
(at least for estimating the mean).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: NUTS questions
messages.body_plain:
Regarding using the entire trajectory rather than just a single point
along it, this can't possibly hurt (I think), and is indeed kosher.
(Although you have to get a little bit subtle to actually prove it.)
But I wouldn't expect it to improve effective sample sizes much at
all, at least for problems where the ESS is significantly less than
the number of iterations. The reason being that the autocorrelations
within a trajectory are going to be pretty enormous. And in the
scenario where it takes many iterations to explore the energy
distribution, taking more samples within a given energy level isn't
going to help with that at all.

Matt

> or so) seems excessive, whereas 2**8 (256) seems
> too small.  I think it should be 2**12 or so.

2**12 = 4096 is a large number of steps compared to what most people have used in practice with HMC before.  It seems reasonable to me, but we could be more conservative and go with 2**16 = 65k.

>
> The problem with making the bound too small is that you
> can get more random walk-like behavior without any warning.
> Making it too large and it can seem to hang, but at
> least you get some feedback that it's having trouble

> and his response to the NUTS paper on his blog), I added the
> option to randomize step size (even after adaptation), which is
> also kosher for detailed balance.  This can be turned on
> independently of NUTS, though Matt doesn't think it'll be necessary
> for NUTS.

My experience has been that the randomized step-size can be rather helpful in finding (and escaping) from narrow parts of the energy landscape where the local curvature is high or changes significantly.  I don't see how this wouldn't be the case with NUTS.  It's probably not the case with an RMHMC type simulation, but who knows.

>
> As to using all the steps of the trajectory, I don't know
> how that would play with detailed balance -- you may
> need to restrict to samples meeting the slicing criterion.

It doesn't impact detailed balance at all as the sampler proceeds in exactly the same way.  The only difference is you keep around the simulation trajectory and a weight which is equal to the probability of accepting that state.  See "An Improved Acceptance Procedure for the hybrid Monte Carlo algorithm" by Neal in J Comp Physics (1994) which discusses this in the context of Neal's windowed acceptance function.

>
> It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
> thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
> (from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
> is that this should improve the effective sample size
> (at least for estimating the mean).

If you're thinning then it's not worth doing this, as the trajectory will be less useful than the thinned samples.  On the flip side, since the NUTS trajectories tend to be long, there seems to be less cause to thin in which case the simulation trajectory could provide some useful information.

Cheers,
Marcus

I'm not sure we're in that big of a danger of a random walk behavior with steps on the order of thousands unless the step-size is miniscule.  Even Langevin Monte Carlo avoids the worst of the Metropolis Hastings random walk behavior with just a single step.

>
> If the model is well behaved, there's no problem with
> a large number of steps because we'll never get that far.

True, but given that it's trivial to specify improper priors in stan, there are certainly ways for the simulation to go off on very long tangents without ever meeting the U-turn condition.  Although I guess this goes back to the standard bugs disclaimer: "Beware: MCMC sampling can be dangerous!"

> And it'll be a good diagnostic to see.

I agree.  The number of steps taken, how often the depth limit is hit and so on are good heuristic diagnostics to report so that users can be aware of potential problems maybe go back to double check their model.

>
> > >    It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
> > >    thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
> > >    (from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
> > >    is that this should improve the effective sample size

>
> I don't understand where weights would come in.
> If we would otherwise have generated five samples,
> thinned to one, and returned it, we could return the
> average of the samples.  It's not that much extra work
> algorithmically.

I think we want to avoid averaging within samples.  It's not always true that averaging even makes sense for some state-spaces.

>
> Do we need weighted averages if we average within
> the leapfrog algorithm?  If we averaged in NUTS, that
> would avoid having to sample one of the points along
> the tractory, right?  I need to go read Radford's paper.

The weights come in as follows:

The standard Monte Carlo estimator of a function f is

E[f(x)] ~= N^-1 \sum_i f(x_i)

Now, assume that x^(1)_i, ..., x^(L)_i is the simulation trajectory starting at sample x_i and that each point along the trajectory had a probability of being selected as the next state which is w^(1)_i, ..., w^(L)_i.  Then the following is also an estimator which has lower variance:

E[f(x)] ~= N^-1 \sum_i \sum_j w^(j)_i f(x^(j)_i)

You're effectively integrating over the choice of the next sample in the estimator instead of only using the one that was chosen when generating the chain.  In traditional HMC it means that you can even use rejected states so long as they're weighted it properly.

The down side of this is that you end up with many more samples and need to do the bookkeeping to keep track of (and use) sample weights which, as Andrew has pointed out, can be a bit tedious and annoying.

At any rate, I'm not sure how we got this far onto this tangent.  Doing this is, at best, a nice-to-have option for stan but certainly isn't necessary.

Cheers,
Marcus

I think you can dynamically load and unload a function called main, but it could potentially name-clash with a function in some other (poorly written) package. R tries to mitigate name clashes by using package namespaces, but in this case the user's model code would be generated by our R package rather than being a part of our R package.

It isn't clear to me how stanc is going to generate C++ code that is suitable for calling from R without some sort of flag. In other words, how would it know to not read the data from the dump file and not take the options from the command line but instead take the data pass-by-reference and options pass-by-value coming from R?

It also seems like it would be feasible to have stanc generate R / MATLAB / Python compatible code without explicitly making dependencies on R / MATLAB / Python. Clearly, the generated C++ code wouldn't run (and possibly not even compile) without them, but users could print the code and stick it on their refrigerators if they wanted.

Ben

We specifically need a class that looks something
like this:

   class r_context : public var_context {
   private:
     Rcpp::Environment _env;
   public:
     r_context(Rcpp::Environment env)
         : _env(env) {
     }

     bool contains_r(const string& var_name);

     ... same thing for integer values ...
   }

I set everything up here to be row-major (and so on
for higher dimensions) so it'd be easy to use from R.

What the command-line invocation does is pass in
a context created out of a var_context created from
a dump, which also implements var_context:

    class dump : public var_context {
    ... some storage ...
    public:
      dump(istream& in) { ... read and store vars ... }

     ...
    }

This reads values from an input stream presumed to
be in S-plus/R "dump" format.

>
> There are a couple of other things that we would need to deal with somehow where stan's current behavior is inconsistent
> with the requirements for R packages.

 > One is that compiled code called from R is not supposed to write to cout or cerr
> because neither is visible to any user who uses any of the various R GUIs. T

The only thing that should be writing to std out and std err
is the command.  The API itself should not have any functions
that ever write to std out or std err.

For instance, the parser stores error info in a string
rather than printing.

 > The R headers define a Rprintf function and
> Rcpp defines Rcout, which should be used. Another situation is error throwing, which has to be done in a particular way
> to avoid crashing the R process. Maybe this can be done with the policy business that I do not understand but a flag was
> the first thing that came to mind.

What we'll do for this is have the R glue code
catch any exceptions thrown by the Stan API and handle
them in a way appropriate to R.  No need to monkey
with any of the underlying code.  That's the beauty of
exceptions if used the right way.

Here's the drill in a nutshell:

1.  Throw an exception if you run into a problem
you can't handle.

2.  If you call a function that throws an exception
you can't handle, pass it on (perhaps catching it first
then throwing an exception of a different type).

3.  If you call a function that throws an exception
you can handle, handle it and don't throw an exception.

This limits the exception throwing to its source
and the handling to some higher level where it can be handled.

The API is written to respect these principles.
If NUTS gets a lower-level math error, it treats it as a 0
probability, handles that case, and doesn't rethrow.
Everything else either just throws (1) or propagates (2).

The command-line invocation of Stan handles exceptions
by catching them and printing them as diagnostics.

The R invocation of Stan will have to handle exceptions in
the same way, reporting errors through R rather than printing
to standard output.

- Bob

No, but I loosely follow sage and they include essentially all GPL2-compatible math software out there. And sage does symbolics with a home-brew python interface to ginac, although they also support sympy as an add-on package.

> My understanding of GPL and BSD "compatibility" is

IANAL, nor have a swallowed a software licensing encyclopedia, and have been told by actual lawyers to STFU many, many times, but that isn't how I would interpret the FSF. I think that link is analogous to what we call "type promotion" in that if you are working on a GPL2+ project and you want to link to a BSD library that is okay because there is nothing in BSD that is inconsistent with GPL2+. But if you are working on a BSD project (like stan) and want to link to a GPL3+ library (like ginac), then the result would be a derived work of the GPL3+ library and need to be licensed under GPL3+. Of course, we could have a separate GPL3+ project that did this or do it internally but not distribute it. My interpretation is based on the first paragraph of

http://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-java.html

> So I was thinking that we'd distribute the rstan code
> with Stan.  Stan remains BSD, but rstan itself must be GPL-ed,
> as it combines Stan (BSD) and R (GPL) code.  I have to check
> again whether we can put rstan on Google Code under those
> conditions, or if we could somehow BSD-license rstan.  It's
> not like we're going to distribute R or other R libraries like Rcpp.

Its hard for me to see how rstan could be anything but GPL2+ due to linking against R and / or Rcpp headers, but I don't know if that means we should separate the repository or host rstan somewhere besides Google Code.

Ben

So the licensing issues of the GPL are based on the idea of a derived work.  If you took R, changed it (e.g., forked it) then you have a derived work and it would have to be GPL.  If, on the other hand, you create a GUI which calls R but does not link to R, then you don't have a derived work and the GUI can have any license it chooses.  The issue of plugins can be tricky, but if they're dynamically loaded and not compiled in, then in general they're not considered derived works.  However, if you use an (R provided) API that makes it easier to write plugins which is GPL, then it is a derived work and it needs to be GPL as well.  If that GPL plugin calls a library which is BSD, then nothing matters.  In essence, so long as the BSD code doesn't call the R API, then it's fine.  As a result, many projects make plugin APIs LGPL or provide explicit exceptions for plugins and external interfaces.  The Linux kernel is one such example of this.

> I just checked and Google code allows GPL v3 (I seem to

E.G., see http://www.dii.unisi.it/hybrid/tools/mex/downloads.html  Certainly there is no license issues which will impact anything other than the MEX glue code.

Marcus

Here is the headers for the API:

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Organization-of-header-files

I think it is technically possible to call dynamically loaded compiled code from R that does not link against the R headers. But the compiled code would not be able to print to R's screen, throw-and-catch errors that get to the user, interrupt long-running jobs, etc. For that reason, the manual says

"The recommended procedure to use these is to include the header file R.h in your C code by #include <R.h>"

whose license is LGPL, as explained

https://svn.r-project.org/R/trunk/doc/COPYRIGHTS

So, rstan couldn't be BSD, although we could make it LGPL. But I was under the impression that we were planning to link against the Rcpp headers, which are GPL2+ only.

Ben

messages.subject: Windows: Building models
messages.body_plain:
We were able to compile the multivariate distributions under windows
by giving cc1plus.exe (part of gcc) more stack space. To do this:
1) Open a command window.
2) Set up the command window to have access to MSDN tools
   - Run: >"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio
10.0\VC\vcvarsall.bat"
3) Find the location of cc1plus.exe and change to that directory:
   - Run: > gcc --print-prog-name cc1plus
   - change directory to the location of the executable
3) See how much stack space is available in cc1plus.exe.
  - Run: > dumpbin /HEADERS cc1plus.exe
4) Edit the stack space
  - Run: > editbin /STACK:10000000 cc1plus.exe

That allows us to run the matrix unit tests and run models. At this
moment, we still have issues building the compiler, stanc. It looks
like a problem with the gnu assembler.

Daniel

messages.subject: log_sum_exp zero-case + tests
messages.body_plain:
The term

     log_sum_exp(0,x)

showed up in the simplex transform when I rearranged
terms to try to prevent overflow.

So I built a special function (and class in auto-dif)
for it.  Here's the definition:

     log1p_exp(x) = log_sum_exp(0,x)

                  = log(exp(0) + exp(x))

                  = log(1 + exp(x))

                  = log1p(exp(x))

and function signatures:

   double stan::math::log1p_exp(double x);

   var stan::agrad::log1p_exp(const var& a);

- Bob

That's an amusing changeset.  x |-> int(x)

I guess they don't like the static_cast<int>(x) idiom.

I think this may have to do with their choice of int
as index type.  This has caused us some issues with
writing templated functions for std::vector and Eigen
with indexing (std::vector uses unsigned int types).
We should probably generalize to iterators anyway.

And of course, all of it's brought on by the fact
that C++ doesn't specify the size of its basic types.

I'm wondering if we should somehow piggyback on
Boost's fixed int sizes.  I know someone brought that
up before.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: write our own auto-dif code gen?
messages.body_plain:
Oops -- just sent this to Matt.  Here's one for
the list.

I've also been meaning to mention that I've
come up with a design for auto-dif that will
take more space (twice the existing space, max),
but won't require any virtual functions.  I'm thinking
it'd be MUCH faster as it'll just execute a very
tight loop.  We can talk about it when you're back.

More comments below.

On 3/24/12 2:19 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> I think this would be great to have, although I agree it's absolutely
> not a priority for Stan 1.0. The obvious advantages are

Right.  NOT for version 1.

> 1. improved compiler optimization
> 2. possibly less memory overhead
> 3. lots more can be put on the stack instead of the heap
> 4. more inlining
> 5. fewer virtual function calls.
> Furthermore, a user who's truly desperate for maximum performance
> could optimize the generated code. Which is a lot easier than starting
> from scratch.
>
> Downsides: it's potentially a lot of work, and it could be a problem
> to call arbitrary functions in other libraries.

Right.  We couldn't re-use exactly what we have, just
its form.  And the big problem is algorithms with
branching and/or iteration.  Other than that ...

> One intermediate option that might make sense to think about is having
> a more limited code gen facility that could play well with the AD
> facility that's currently in place. We could use that to automatically
> generate, e.g., log-probability vari classes that implement the
> appropriate chain() functions. E.g., we could generate a
> normal_vvv_vari class, a normal_vvd_vari class, etc., each of which
> does all of the work that is currently being done by calling the
> square(), operator/, operator-, operator*, log() functions and their
> corresponding chain() functions. These normal_xxx_vari's would produce
> the same results, but with dramatically fewer calls to the various
> chain() functions.
>
> Just a thought.

Absolutely!

That's what I've been saying from the get go.  The best place
for optimization in the current design is in partial evaluation
of the derivatives in the log probability functions and in the
matrix functions.

We could also help with numerical stability by adding more
basic distributions expressed directly in terms of the unconstrained
parameters, like

    bernoulli_logit(x|alpha) =def= bernoulli(x|ilogit(alpha))

Everything's pretty stable at this point (other than the builds
on various different compilers), so it's OK with me if anyone wants
to go ahead and start doing that.  Just make sure to add all the
tests.  Our API doc's all over the place, so I'm not so worried about
that at this point.

I know Ben wanted to do some other multivariate distribution
parameterizations.

I'm in the middle of writing the manual.  Which is actually a lot
of fun.

- Bob

messages.subject: explicit instantiation for template compilation
messages.body_plain:
I tracked through some old mail on the parser board
which pointed in this direction and then
re-read Vandevoorde and Josuttis template book on
translation units and compilation strategies, and
I think we should try the explicit instantiation
approach to deal with our current scaling issues with
compilation (Eigen matrix lib w. auto-dif and in the
parser for the Stan modeling language).

To illustrate the approach, I pushed a new directory

   stan/src/demo/templ_inst_demo

There's a README which shows how to split what
we have in a single header file (.hpp) into
a declaration-only header and a definition header,
then define and compile explicit template instantations.
Other libraries compile against the declaration-only
header and then get linked to the result of compiling
the template instantiations.  We could probably
even put different instantiations in different files.

The nice part is, we get our existing header-only usage
pattern by including the definition headers.

- Bob

It does seem like it'd be possible to auto-generate
some of this code.  But then I'm a computer scientist,
so I'm an easy sell on automation.

There are a couple (OK, a few) things to keep in mind.

1.  We need 2^N signatures for an N-ary function to
efficiently handle all the ways it might get instantiated.
Some of those you might skip because they'll be efficient
as handled now, or perhaps just not called very often.

2.  The biggest savings come from clever algebra in
the gradient calc that can eliminate or combine subexpression
calculations.

Having said that, the densities aren't too bad the way they
are, but there's definitely room for speedup.

3.  Vectorization is totally different.  If we have
a whole bunch of normal observations, we only need
to compute log(sigma) once, and that's a huge savings.
You don't even need clever algebra here -- just a little
summation.

4.  Where we're really inefficient now is in things
like dot-products.  That stores a gazillion intermediate
expressions of type vari on the stack.

- Bob

messages.subject: new auto-dif design
messages.body_plain:
The basic idea of the new design is rather like
more traditional designs.  The goal is to get rid
of the virtual function calls during derivative
propagation.  And no, just using function pointers doesn't
help -- that's where Matt started.  We need to get
rid of the whole concept.

The idea would be to instead store the expression graph
qua graph on a stack-like structure.

Each subexpression needs to store:

    - value
    - adjoint
    - list of subexpressions
    - list of partials with respect to subexpressions

There are many ways to do this.

I've been thinking of storing it pretty literally
as a graph, with nodes for expressions represented by three
parallel arrays:

     double[] values;
     double[] adjs;
     int[] first_edge_idx; // index into array of edges

The edges then store the partials and the value of
the dtrs in another pair of parallel arrays:

     int[] expr_index;   // index into array of nodes
     double[] partial;

For instance, expression 7 would have value
values[7], adjoint adjs[7], and dtr expressions
ranging from first_edge_idx[7] (inclusive) to
first_edge_idx[8] (exclusive) {this is a standard
trick for packing because we know the subexpressions
are contiguous, so we don't need both a start and
an end pointer, we can just have a start pointer and
use the next expression's start pointer as an exclusive
end pointer).

Then the partials need to get stored as a double value
and added to the stack.

Derivative propagation is now super easy, as it just
goes down the node stack, and for each expression,
iterates through its subexpression adding the expression's
adjoint times the partial w.r.t. the subexpression to the
subexpression's adjoint.

The equivalent of var now holds an index into the stack
of nodes, making it simple to compute value() and adj()
There is no longer a class for vari.  That could
make var shorter if we can go with int (max out at 2G or
so subexpressions).

In fact, we could probably get rid of the values[] in
the node stack if we pushed the value into var itself.
It makes copying var heavier (not so good), but could save
lots of storage (very good).

- Bob

That would certainly lead to clean derivative code.

Unfortunately, it would take up way more space.
The method I was suggesting is packed pretty tightly
into memory.  Not as tightly as the current approach,
but close.

Check out the implementations of the Eigen objects.

I'm suggesting going a level lower representationally
than Eigen or std::vector.

> Question: How would the proposed design generalize to Hessians? In the old design, I thought it was approximately just a
> matter of making the derivatives into vars and differentiating them again.

Doing reverse-mode auto-dif twice works conceptually.
You essentially auto-dif the evaluation of the first-pass
dif to get the second derivatives.

But given that forward-mode auto-dif is so much
ligher memory wise, it's better to compute Hessians
row-wise and compute forward auto-dif for one dimension
of output and reverse-mode auto-dif that.  Forward-mode
doesn't need any allocation and is much easier to template.

In fact, templated forward-mode is much easier than
reverse mode.  I implemented the basics a while ago.

Matt's thinking about doing something a bit different, I think,
which would instead of computing a Hessian, would compute
a Hessian-gradient product.  That I haven't looked into closely.

> But, in general, I would say implement first (in a branch), ask questions later. If you do it and it turns out to be 1%
> faster, then I am basically sold.

Definitely the way to go for any kind of major change.

I'm pretty sure what I'm proposing will be more than 1%
faster.    It does the same arithmetic but without
any virtual function calls -- just a tight loop.  It
does read in a bit more memory, which will slow it down.

Right now, we're being lazy in computing the partials
as we need them during derivative propagation.  That
saves the space that the new proposal uses to store all
the partials in the forward evaluation.  The benefit of
storing them all is that there's no thinking (virtual
function calls) in the reverse step.

It's partly a scalability vs. efficiency call.  Though
we don't know exactly what either of those two will look
like in real use cases.

- Bob

> of the virtual function calls during derivative
> propagation.  And no, just using function pointers doesn't
> help -- that's where Matt started.  We need to get
> rid of the whole concept.

Right, the performance hit with virtual functions comes from a function call that the compiler can't optimize because it's defined at run time.  Virtual functions are basically implemented with function pointers, so that doesn't surprise me.  There's also the added memory hit with virtual functions for the vtable pointer.  I don't actually think your scheme below will increase memory usage that much overall since most expressions only have one or two subexpressions but you're saving at least one 64bit pointers worth of memory per expression.  So maybe a 50% increase in memory.

For reference, I'm running a model right now which has ~40k variables and top reports it using around 1G of memory.  I would consider that to be pretty reasonable and even doubling it for a large boost in performance would definitely be worth it.

>
> The idea would be to instead store the expression graph
> qua graph on a stack-like structure.
>
> Each subexpression needs to store:
>
>   - value
>   - adjoint
>   - list of subexpressions
>   - list of partials with respect to subexpressions
>
> There are many ways to do this.
>
> I've been thinking of storing it pretty literally
> as a graph, with nodes for expressions represented by three
> parallel arrays:
>
>    double[] values;
>    double[] adjs;
>    int[] first_edge_idx; // index into array of edges
>
> The edges then store the partials and the value of
> the dtrs in another pair of parallel arrays:
>
>    int[] expr_index;   // index into array of nodes
>    double[] partial;
>
> For instance, expression 7 would have value
> values[7], adjoint adjs[7], and dtr expressions
> ranging from first_edge_idx[7] (inclusive) to
> first_edge_idx[8] (exclusive) {this is a standard
> trick for packing because we know the subexpressions
> are contiguous, so we don't need both a start and
> an end pointer, we can just have a start pointer and
> use the next expression's start pointer as an exclusive
> end pointer).
>
> Then the partials need to get stored as a double value
> and added to the stack.
>
> Derivative propagation is now super easy, as it just
> goes down the node stack, and for each expression,
> iterates through its subexpression adding the expression's
> adjoint times the partial w.r.t. the subexpression to the
> subexpression's adjoint.
>
> The equivalent of var now holds an index into the stack
> of nodes, making it simple to compute value() and adj()
> There is no longer a class for vari.  That could
> make var shorter if we can go with int (max out at 2G or
> so subexpressions).

It might be worth making the type of index a compile-time option since an int is likely plenty for small models, but could come up short for really big ones.

I'm not sure how this saves memory, as you still need to store a double for every var.  It's just been moved from the node stack to the var.  Or did I miss something?

The vtable pointer in the case of vari, since it has
only one virtual function, is exactly the size of a function
pointer.  It's just much more convenient to use.

> I don't actually think your
> scheme below will increase memory usage that much overall since most
> expressions only have one or two subexpressions but you're saving at
> least one 64bit pointers worth of memory per expression.  So maybe a 50%

Not quite.  Here's the memory rundown for an
expression with N subexpressions or arguments
under both schemes.

   Current Scheme:

   var
   8      pointer to vari
   -----
   8

   vari
   8      vtable pointer to chain()
   8      value
   8      adjoint
   8N     pointers to all N subexpressions
   --------
   24 + 8N

   New Scheme (indexed by long / int)

   var
   8  / 4  ptr to expression table
   -------
   8 / 4

   expression (node) table
   8        value
   8        adjoint
   8 / 4    pointer to first subexpression

   partial (edge) table
   8N       value
   8N / 4N  pointers to var subexpressions  table
   ----------
   24 + 16N / 20 + 12N

Breaking that down by expression arity:

            Now   New(8)   New(4)
   0-ary:   24     24       20
   1-ary:   32     40       32
   2-ary:   40     56       44
   3-ary:   48     72       56

   N-ary:  24+8N  24+16N   20+12N

So it's more expensive in memory.  Not enough
to really worry about for basic ops.  For
instance, the normal distribution is 3-ary.

Three caveats.

1.  The new scheme only needs to store subexpressions
that are vars.   This could lead to lots of savings
in some cases.

2.  Think of dot product of two K-dimensional matrices
as an example.  Once we optimize vector expressions
by giving them auto-dif classes, this'll be one class
that stores pointers to the two vectors themselves.
This means the old scheme will only use 40 bytes.
The new scheme will store them all.  Even if K=20,
we'll need over 300 bytes even if one of the vectors
is a double rather than a var.

3.  The implicit end-of-subexpressions coding I'm
using means that memory needs to be allocated so
that the node arrays and edge arrays are just one big
array.  That'll require either pre-allocating big,
or copying during resize.  Our current scheme has slightly
better properties for this.

Thanks for making me reason through all of this!

You could use a deque to avoid the large contiguous memory requirement. This might just be my Matlab background talking, but it seems to me
like it'd be best to have everything be vectorized every which way.
And the suggestion about using multivariate distributions makes sense
in the context of the normal, but less so for distributions that don't
have such a natural multivariate analog (e.g. gamma, Poisson, etc.).
It's a pain (and somewhat error-prone) to try to code up 4 or 8
versions of every density (16 if we support the generalized
inverse-Gaussian), which is why I suggested that it'd be nice to have
a way of generating them automatically.

It seems to me like there shouldn't necessarily be an obstacle to
getting (relatively) efficient implementations automatically, at least
if we're comparing with what we're doing now. Probably they won't be
100% optimal, but they should at least be better than using autodiff
for intermediate adjoint calculations and throwing a bunch of varis on
the heap. Although that may be less true once Bob's finished the new
autodiff implementation.

Best,
Matt

On 3/27/12 5:39 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> This might just be my Matlab background talking,

It's a bit different in C++ than in R or MATLAB.
There's no cost for iteration/access in the C++
world (or in the compiled Stan world for that matter).

On the other hand, sometimes the vectorization is
a huge savings if you can consolidate operations.
For instance, the kind of thing Ben was talking about
for a Cholesky representation along the lines of
Eigen's LLT class.

 > but it seems to me
> like it'd be best to have everything be vectorized every which way.

The problem is that vectorizing can really hurt
you if you do too many allocations/constructions or
indirections as a result.  It was the motivating
case for the development of expression templates!

What you don't want to do is encourage people to write
this:

    vector x, u, v;
    double c;
    x = u + c * v;

if you're going to have to allocate an intermediate vector
to represent (c * v).  You're better off with the for loop:

    for (i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)
        x[i] = u[i] + c * v[i];

With expression templates, as used in Eigen, you can get
code almost this efficient while writing it in vectorized
forms (and in other cases, much more efficient code from
writing in vectorized form).  You get an expression template
for scalar multiplication class on the stack pointing
to (c,v) and another one pointing to (u[i],(c,v)).  Then
operator[](int) works out to be defined like x[i] above
once all the dust settles.

Now here's the real problem.  In order to get the advantages
of both expression templates *and* partial evaluation of
derivatives, we'll have to

(a) rewrite Eigen to support mixed-type binary ops;  they're
up for it, but I'm not sure we are

(b) push the auto-dif partial evaluations through to the Eigen's
expression templates

The way stan::agrad::matrix is implemented now, we can only
get the advantages of partial evaluation of derivatives.
Just adding mixed binary types to Eigen only gives us the
advantage of expression templates.  We need to do both (a) and
(b) to get both.

The bigger speedup will come from partially evaluating
the auto-dif, because of all the memory manipulation savings.
(And it's not just the malloc time, it's the time to put things
on the stack, run their constructors, and then run their virtual chain()
methods.)

> And the suggestion about using multivariate distributions makes sense
> in the context of the normal, but less so for distributions that don't
> have such a natural multivariate analog (e.g. gamma, Poisson, etc.).
> It's a pain (and somewhat error-prone) to try to code up 4 or 8
> versions of every density (16 if we support the generalized
> inverse-Gaussian), which is why I suggested that it'd be nice to have
> a way of generating them automatically.

I agree.  The reason they're not all unfolded
every which way now is the pain and errorfulness of doing
it.  I'm still hoping to nail down version 1 before
any of this.

> It seems to me like there shouldn't necessarily be an obstacle to
> getting (relatively) efficient implementations automatically, at least
> if we're comparing with what we're doing now. Probably they won't be
> 100% optimal, but they should at least be better than using autodiff
> for intermediate adjoint calculations and throwing a bunch of varis on
> the heap. Although that may be less true once Bob's finished the new
> autodiff implementation.

I'm not even sure the new auto-dif idea is a good one.
See the last message.  It'll depend on the balance of
multivariate and univariate ops.  The "new" auto-dif is
actually closer to some of the other versions out
there than what's in Stan.  Stan's is based on Matt's
original function-pointer version, which stored pointers
to the daughters the same way the classes do now.  I converted
it to an OO rep and built out the library and implemented
all the operators.  What's neat is that we really leaned on
the optimizing compiler to do it -- compared to CppAD, another
tool out there, Stan runs a bit faster at -O3 than CppAD at -O3,
but about half as slow at -O0.  CppAD is full of case statements,
making it very hard to extend, too.  Whereas Stan now has
drop-in auto-dif extensions.

I need to doc what needs to be done to drop in a user-defined
function and/or auto-dif calculation, but it's totally possible
with the existing Stan language.

- Bob

Stan.

messages.subject: name/behavior for CODA-like object?
messages.body_plain:
Daniel's starting in on the convergence monitoring
for Stan.

I'm leaning toward "epilog(ue)" as a name.
It's the literary equivalent of a coda in
music.

The other issue is how to build it.  Right now,
we're thinking it'll be easiest to have Stan
work the way it does now, writing to files in
different processes.  Then the Epilogue object
reads them in and stores them much like Coda
does.   See the P.S. for two other alternatives.

Anyway, we then need methods for:

   -- access underlying data in a (structured) way
   -- get number of chains
   -- get names (and dimensions) of parameters
   -- effective sample size (variogram estimates)
   -- smallest posterior intervals
   -- central posterior intervals
   -- split R-hat
   -- print method like R's coda print method

It'd be nice to have:

   -- constructor reading from istream (e.g., file input stream)
   -- method writing to ostream

I think that's pretty much everything we've talked about.

Coda in addition gives you:

   -- cross-parameter correlations
   -- auto-correlation within chain (or combined chain) methods

And to access it from the command line, we'll need
a command to read in data and print a report.

Having an object will make it pretty easy to access
from R using Rcpp modules.  The plotting methods all go
on the R side, which again, we're putting off in favor
of writing the C++.

- Bob

P.S.
The alternative would be to figure out
multi-threading in some way that is portable and
write all the samples into a single object in
a single process in memory.  This has the advantage
of likely being faster, but the disadvantage of
adding to our compatibility woes (threading in C++
wasn't even remotely standardized until C++11, but
R doesn't give us recent enough compilers to deal
with C++11).

P.P.S.
An even more ambitious alternative would be to
have it be online, multithreaded and do some kind
of on-the-fly convergence monitoring.  I really
liked Andrew's logarithmic deepening suggestion
for computing split R-hat on the fly, which is the
only tricky thing.  We could store accumulators
for stats split at even powers of 2^N:

   1--32, 33--64,
   1--128, 129--256
   1--256, 257--512,
   ...
   1--2^N, 2^N+1--2^(N+1)

Then we can compute split R-hat exactly when we
hit 64, 128, 256, samples.  The neat bit is that
the 1--128 just comes about from merging 1--32
and 33--64, so we don't ever need that many
accumulators running at once.  Think of all the
indexing fun implementing this!

On 3/30/12 5:42 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I'd prefer to avoid a bank-shot reference like that.

Is this the same nominal genius (I hope everyone
got that linguistic pun) that brought us "Stan"?

 > I'd rather just call it a stan object and keep things simple.

We only need a clever name if we're going to
have a standalone package in the way that Coda
stands alone from R2Jags or R2WinBUGS.

Even then, from a branding point of view, I can
see big advantages in keeping everything under
one name or family of related names (and no,
I don't think "Nick" would work [after Metropolis]).

I saw in looking at R2Jags, that you don't even
doc the return type of the jags() function.  And it
doesn't get standalone object doc, either.  So
you cleverly avoided the naming problem there.

But let's call ours "mcmc_output" for want of a better
name, because we have too many different kind of objects
to get much use out of "stan object" as a description.

Aside from naming, modularity is good and good
for you -- it helps manage the complexity of a big
project by defining small, well-defined units that
can be understood, tested, and maintained separately.

We'll build the mcmc_output object so that it only
requires a set of chains (either online or batch) to
construct.  It won't know anything about NUTS
any more than Coda knows anything about Gibbs or
Metropolis.  (If we did need something that knew
about NUTS specifically, we'd add more independent
functions or a subclass of mcmc_output called
nuts_output.)

The overall command-line program will then hold
a reference to the Stan sampler and a reference to
the mcmc output object.  It will then pull samples
from the sampler and use them to populate the output,
which it will either pump back to R or use to
write to file.

- Bob

messages.subject: stan syntax
messages.body_plain:
How set in stone is stan syntax at this date?

As a case in point, lately I've been writing BUGS/JAGS models, and I
came across this inconsistency.

If you have a univariate normal parameter, you can write:

   alpha ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)

If you have a multivariate normal parameter, you have to write:

   alpha ~ dmnorm(mu[], tau[,])

and then you have to define mu[] and tau[,] in the data that you pass to
BUGS. It'd be more convenient and consistent to define mu[] and tau[,]
directly in the model file, not in the data.

messages.subject: Re: stan syntax
messages.body_plain:
I don't think anything in stan is set in stone, but the stan syntax already avoids your complains about BUGS / JAGS.

If mu and / or Sigma (covariance matrix) are parameters, then you can define them in the parameters, transformed parameters, or model sections. For example,

parameters {
  cov_matrix(K) Sigma;
}

where K is known and defined in the data section. There are several choices for a prior density for Sigma in stan.

You might use the transformed parameters section if you wanted a covariance matrix for an AR1 process where Sigma is a function of rho and sigma^2. You might use the model section if you considered Sigma to be a nuisance parameter and didn't want to store the draws for it.

If mu and tau (precision matrix) are fixed constants, then you can define them in the data or transformed data sections. Actually, at the moment we do not have a version of the multivariate normal density that takes a precision matrix, so your code would be much faster if you increment the log posterior yourself in the model section with something like

lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * (x - mu)' * tau * (x - mu);

when both x and mu are defined as vectors.

Eventually, we will probably add convenience functions for AR1, multivariate normal parameterized with a precision matrix, etc. But in the meantime, stan is certainly capable of letting the user implement these things manually.

Ben

On Saturday, March 31, 2012 9:45:09 AM UTC-4, jacktanner wrote:

> came across this inconsistency.

> If you have a univariate normal parameter, you can write:
>
>    alpha ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
>
> If you have a multivariate normal parameter, you have to write:
>
>    alpha ~ dmnorm(mu[], tau[,])
>
> and then you have to define mu[] and tau[,] in the data that you pass to
> BUGS. It'd be more convenient and consistent to define mu[] and tau[,]
> directly in the model file, not in the data.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: stan syntax
messages.body_plain:
The syntax isn't set in stone.  But it's
pretty solid at this point.  I'm writing up
that part of the manual over the weekend so things
will be clearer.

As Ben says, you can define constants in the
"transformed data" section of the model file,
which is for any variables that can be defined
solely in terms of the variables in the "data" block
or earlier in the "transformed data" block.

Also, you won't need the brackets.  It'll look
like:

   transformed data {
       covar_matrix(2) Sigma;
       vector(2) mu;

       Sigma[1,1] <- 1.7;
       Sigma[2,2] <- 1.3;
       Sigma[1,2] <- 0.4;
       Sigma[2,1] <- Sigma[1,2];

       mu[1] <- 3.7;
       mu[2] <- -14.2;
   }
   model {
       y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
       ...
   }

I keep thinking I should add a literal assignment syntax for
matrices, to allow something like:

     Sigma <- ((1,7. 0.4),
               (0.4, 1.3));

     mu <- (3.7, -14.2);

or even a general expression that would allow variables
or other expressions as well as constants.

It's on the to-do list, but I'm in the middle
of trying to refactor the parser to break it into
multiple translation units to ease the burden on
the C++ compilers and assemblers.

We'll also be adding other parameterizations and vectorized
versions for multiple samples.

We will try very very hard to keep the model syntax
backwards compatible.

You can look in the directory of BUGS examples for more
examples of Stan's syntax.

- Bob

On Saturday, March 31, 2012 3:37:16 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Is it OK with everyone if we only support the latest
> version of R?  There's a new one out as of yesterday,
> 2.15, and they changed versions of GCC.
>

There are "hard" and "soft" version requirements for R, and I would be fine with a soft one. In other words, we can say in the README or whatever that stan will (eventually) work on the latest released version of R *for Windows*, presumably with the latest released version of Rtools. This is not too much of a burden because it is pretty easy to update R on a personal Windows machine.

Alternatively, the hard route would require a certain version of R for *all operating systems* by specifying R 2.15 in the Requires section of the DESCRIPTION file. I think this would be overkill because it would preclude Linux / Mac / Solaris / etc. users with older versions of R but new enough versions of g++ from using stan. And these people are more likely to be using R via a server where they may not have administrative rights to update R.

> On 3/31/12 3:17 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Saturday, March 31, 2012 1:47:45 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The toolchain Rtools215.exe is listed as "not frozen".
>

>
> And do you think 215 is the one to use?

215 is definitely the one to use in conjunction with the latest R. The timestamps on the files inside multi.zip are mostly December with a few January. It may become frozen by the time rstan is released.

> And what in the world do they mean by "releases after 2.14.1 will
> use a new toolchain based on pre-4.6.3 gcc"?  Are they really
> using a pre-relese version of an old GCC?

Yes, although I don't know why. I am guessing that they cannot afford downtime on the CRAN servers so if they find a version of a compiler that mostly works with all 3000 R packages they have to build and rebuild, then they stick with it until forced to upgrade.

> > Also, I thought I got Jenkins working again last night ("Jenkins build is back to normal") but this morning it says it

On Mar 31, 2012, at 1:02 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On 3/30/12 5:42 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> I'd prefer to avoid a bank-shot reference like that.
>
> Is this the same nominal genius (I hope everyone
> got that linguistic pun) that brought us "Stan"?
>
> > I'd rather just call it a stan object and keep things simple.
>
> We only need a clever name if we're going to
> have a standalone package in the way that Coda
> stands alone from R2Jags or R2WinBUGS.
>
> Even then, from a branding point of view, I can
> see big advantages in keeping everything under
> one name or family of related names (and no,
> I don't think "Nick" would work [after Metropolis]).
>
> I saw in looking at R2Jags, that you don't even
> doc the return type of the jags() function.  And it
> doesn't get standalone object doc, either.  So
> you cleverly avoided the naming problem there.
>
> But let's call ours "mcmc_output" for want of a better
> name, because we have too many different kind of objects
> to get much use out of "stan object" as a description.
>
> Aside from naming, modularity is good and good
> for you -- it helps manage the complexity of a big
> project by defining small, well-defined units that
> can be understood, tested, and maintained separately.
>
> We'll build the mcmc_output object so that it only
> requires a set of chains (either online or batch) to
> construct.  It won't know anything about NUTS
> any more than Coda knows anything about Gibbs or
> Metropolis.  (If we did need something that knew
> about NUTS specifically, we'd add more independent
> functions or a subclass of mcmc_output called
> nuts_output.)
>
> The overall command-line program will then hold
> a reference to the Stan sampler and a reference to
> the mcmc output object.  It will then pull samples
> from the sampler and use them to populate the output,
> which it will either pump back to R or use to
> write to file.
>
> - Bob
